item.title: Unified Charge-Transfer Diagrams for Teaching Molecule-Surface Interactions
Optical Properties of Different Chemistries of Natural and Synthetic Melanin
item.description: Melanin, a ubiquitous black pigment, consists of at least five chemistries identified by the starting monomers involved in its polymerization. Natural melanin may also contain other components, such as lipids and proteins, that can affect its optical properties. Melanin is known for its high refractive index and broadband absorption. However, most optical-property observations are based on measurements of eumelanin-based chemistry. In this study, we used spectroscopic ellipsometry to measure the complex refractive index over a broad wavelength range (380–1700 nm) for the three main melanin chemistries: eumelanin, allomelanin, and pheomelanin. We compared the complex refractive indices of these materials with values obtained from UV absorption measurements, using an integrating sphere to minimize scattering effects. Our results show that melanin chemistry strongly influences optical properties. Pheomelanin from human red hair has the lowest absorption and refractive index, while poly(L-3,4-dihydroxyphenylalanine) (PDOPA; a polydopamine-based eumelanin chemistry) has the highest refractive index and absorption. We also observed variation in the optical properties of pheomelanin samples extracted from human red hair and rooster feathers. Thus, variations in melanin composition affect both the optical and thermal properties of melanin, highlighting the need to identify its precise chemistry in natural systems to understand melanin's impact on function and performance.

item.title: Multi-Criteria Decision-Making Framework for Sustainable Engineering Materials: Integrating Biopolymer Structure, Processing, Properties, Scalability, Techno-Economics, and Life-Cycle Assessment
item.description: Renewable biopolymers are often compared by feedstock origin, biodegradability, or isolated properties, yet an engineering decision concerns a biopolymer processed into a de-fined architecture for a specified application under practical manufacturing constraints. This study develops a multi-criteria decision-making framework for alginate, cellulose, lignin, chitosan, and starch in which the decision unit is a material–processing route–architecture–application system. Each unit is scored on molecular functionality, pro-cessing compatibility, architecture, application-relevant performance, and scalability, with independent evidence-confidence flags, explicit treatment of missing evidence, and bal-anced, performance-led, and manufacturability-led weighting scenarios. Techno-economic and life-cycle evidence is retained as a separate confidence and constraint layer. Fourteen decision units were evaluated from published literature across three contrasting demon-stration cases. Four units were classified as evidence-limited, converting data gaps into explicit research priorities. The framework provides a reproducible, transferable bridge between qualitative renewable-biopolymer reviews and application-specific materi-al-system design.

item.title: JAI: Physically Constrained Prediction of Conformer-Averaged Proton–Proton Coupling Constants in Solution
item.description: Machine-learning predictors of proton–proton coupling constants are usually trained on, and evaluated against, couplings computed for single geometries rather than the conformer-averaged values measured in solution. We describe JAI (J-coupling prediction with Artificial Intelligence), a graph transformer for 2J–5J(H,H) of small organic molecules trained on scaled Fermi-contact DFT couplings of about 3700 molecules, computed on geometries from the universal machine-learned potential UMA and averaged over conformers in six solvents, and on more than 25 000 curated experimental couplings annotated with their uncertainty, sign provenance and assignment. A fast mode predicts from the structure diagram; a conformer mode supplies, for each conformer of a reproducible search, the coefficients of Karplus-type expressions that are averaged with predicted populations; and a weighted combination of the two gives the final output, with 68 % and 90 % intervals calibrated on cross-validation errors. Against experimental couplings, the combined output reaches a mean absolute error of 0.43 Hz in cross-validation and 0.55 Hz when all compounds from the same literature source are held out together, our most realistic estimate for new chemistry. It reaches 0.35 Hz on 335 held-out compounds (fast mode: 0.53 Hz in cross-validation and 0.43 Hz on these compounds) and 0.57 Hz on 132 compounds added after the model had been finalized, 37 of them with environments that have very few DFT training examples. For vicinal couplings between sp3 carbons, it lowers the cross-validated error from 0.85 Hz with the fast mode to 0.66 Hz. The intervals hold for compounds like those of the training data but are too narrow for rare chemistry. item.title: Synthesis of a Molecular Four-Ring Brunnian Link
item.description: Mathematics describes infinitely many distinct knots and links, but translating these topologies into molecular structures remains a major challenge in chemistry. Here, we develop a strategy to bridge mathematical topology and molecular synthesis using single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), with a four-ring Brunnian link (4-BL) as a demanding test case. Because cutting any one ring releases all the others, the Brunnian property can be directly verified by selective cleavage. By surveying existing Brunnian link constructions and screening a census of links with up to fourteen crossings, we identified only one 4-BL type at fourteen crossings. Because a link can may have different diagrams, which impose different constraints on molecular construction, we developed a computational method to search for alternative minimal diagrams. We identified four distinct 14-crossing diagrams for the 4-BL, from which we selected one best suited to molecular construction based on their geometrical properties. The chirality and directionality of ssDNA make all fourteen crossings symmetry-distinct. To achieve precise control over the positions, connectivity and handednesses of these crossings, we reversed the orientation of one helical strand in the canonical DNA tensegrity triangle (cTT), whose crossings all have the same sign, to develop two additional motifs: the reverse TT (rTT), containing parallel junctions, and the inverted TT (iTT), containing bowtie junctions with artificial 5′–5′ and 3′–3′ linkages. We combined cTT, rTT and iTT to synthesize the 4-BL and verified its topology by enzymatic cleaving each ring. We further found that, unlike the three-ring Borromean rings, the 4-BL relaxes through multiple intermediates under the action of E. coli topoisomerase I before complete unlinking, consistent with our computational strand-passage analysis. Our work demonstrates how mathematical link analysis can guide the construction of experimentally verifiable molecular topologies and provides new structural motifs for extending programmable DNA assembly to more complex molecular entanglements.

item.title: False Confidence in Generative Samplers: Exact Physical References Expose Hidden Errors and Diagnostic Blindness
Collision Cross Section Measurement within Time-of-Flight and Multi-Reflection Analyzers
item.description: A proportion of ions travelling through a time-of-flight analyzer inevitably suffer collisions with background gas, resulting in unwanted transmission losses. As collision probability depends upon the ions’ collision cross section, it has been considered that measurement of ion transmission with variation of pressure, or flight path in the case of some multi-reflection analyzers, allows cross section to be determined. A theoretical model is presented, and practical evaluations performed upon a Thermo Scientific Orbitrap Astral mass spectrometer.

item.title: A Staged Reaction Optimisation Workflow for Fragment-to-Lead Elaboration
item.description: Here, we present a reaction optimisation workflow that integrates data mining to generate unbiased, data-led starting points, high-throughput experimentation (HTE) to narrow the reaction parameter space, and closed-loop flow experiments guided by multi-objective Bayesian optimisation for fine-tuning. Designed for early-stage medicinal chemistry, particularly fragment-based drug discovery (FBDD), the workflow was demonstrated in two direct two-step syntheses of potent fragment-derived protein kinase C inhibitor precursors, involving sequential C–C and C–X bond formations. Quantum-mechanical (QM) reactivity prediction was used to inform route redesign improving synthetic efficiency and safety. HTE identified promising categorical starting points, which were subsequently refined within 20-40 autonomous continuous flow experiments per campaign, across 4 reaction steps. The workflow improved reaction yields in both syntheses while minimising simple E-factor and incorporating selectivity as an additional optimisation objective to facilitate downstream purification. An accelerated variant identified comparably productive conditions within a single working week, reducing substrate consumption by approximately 60%. This work demonstrates how staged, data-informed optimisation can accelerate material delivery in early-stage drug discovery while reducing experimental burden and providing valuable insights for subsequent process optimisation.

item.title: Laser-Assisted Nuclear Thermal Propulsion for Cislunar Logistics: A Monte Carlo Power-Closure Assessment
item.description: Laser-assisted nuclear thermal propulsion (LANTP) would raise the specific impulse of a nuclear thermal tug by adding orbital laser power to the hydrogen. We take performance targets of this kind (specific impulse 1300–1500 s, thrust 50–120 kN, a 1–50 MW laser on a 100–500 MWt reactor, and an initial mass in low Earth orbit, IMLEO, 40% below that of conventional nuclear thermal propulsion, NTP) as hypothetical design targets and test them for Earth–Moon logistics with a coupled model: hydrogen thermochemistry checked against Cantera, a power chain from the wall plug to the propellant, Gaussian-beam capture, finite burns with occultation and link dropouts, tug and laser-node masses, and Monte Carlo and Sobol analyses over assumed ranges. Reaching 1300–1500 s requires a useful laser power of 2.2–3.6 times the reactor power, so a 1–50 MW laser gives at most 1,000 s, and 50–120 kN needs 0.7–1.6 GW of emitted power. Against a conventional tug whose reactor is sized for the payload, the laser-assisted tug has a median IMLEO ratio of 1.44 (5th–95th percentile 1.13–1.94); 0% of the draws are below 1 and none reaches 0.6. Receiver specific mass accounts for 70% of the variance. A technology-threshold map shows that a mass benefit needs a receiver below approximately 11 kg per MW absorbed. 2 The laser nodes (about 18 kt) and the propellant reserve for a single laser fault eliminate this benefit. Results are conditional on the assumed ranges.

item.title: Atomically Precise Au22(Lys-Cys-Lys)16 Gold Nanocluster as Type I Photosensitizer: ROS Generation Mechanism
item.description: The exceptional response of the gold nanocluster Au22(Lys-Cys-Lys)16, capable of generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) via electron transfer, was studied from both computational modeling and experimental characterization. An electron density perspective on remarkable features of gold nanoclusters and their photophysical applications provides a comprehensive study of the mechanism the gold nanocluster Au22(Lys-Cys-Lys)16 undergoes as a type I photosensitizer. By means of molecular dynamics simulations, density functional theory for ground state and excited states, and linear response - time dependent density functional theory calculations, the optical properties of the nanocluster and its interactions in aqueous media were studied. Analysis of frontier molecular orbitals of Au22(Lys-Cys-Lys)16 revealed that this nanocluster can transfer an electron from the gold core to a dioxygen molecule in the vicinity, generating ROS by following a spin-flip transition. The results suggest a strong connection between redistribution of electron density in the excited state and the ability of Au22(Lys-Cys-Lys)16 to act as an electron donor rather than as a more commonly studied energy transfer mechanism for gold nanoclusters, mainly reported as photosensitizers type II. This study also probes the underlying mechanism of fluorescence quenching in aqueous media providing a comprehensive description of the experimental detection of ROS at different pH.

item.title: Predictive Modeling of Friction-Resistant Advanced Coatings using Fluid Dynamics
item.description: Turbulent skin-friction resistance in industrial conduit transport and piping infrastructure accounts for substantial energy dissipation worldwide. Biomimetic shark-skin riblets offer an attractive passive drag-reduction mechanism by constraining cross-stream turbulent momentum transfer and pinning quasi-streamwise vortices aloft. However, optimizing these micro-topographies across high-dimensional parameter spaces (riblet spacing s, aspect ratio h/s, conduit diameter D, and Reynolds number Re) remains experimentally and numerically prohibitive owing to the computational expense of high-fidelity Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD). In this study, we established a deterministic, high-throughput machine learning surrogate framework to accelerate the predictive design of friction-resistant advanced coatings. A space-filling 4-dimensional design matrix spanning s ∈ [10, 120] μm, h/s ∈ [0.20, 1.20], D ∈ [25.1, 249.8] mm, and Re ∈ [10,000, 200,000] was generated via Quasi-Monte Carlo (QMC) Latin Hypercube Sampling (N = 1,000 geometries). An automated execution pipeline coupled Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) k-ω SST turbulence modeling with near-wall Navier slip boundary conditions, benchmarked against classical Petukhov analytical theory with relative baseline discretization errors below ±0.4%. An ensemble Random Forest regressor (300 bootstrapped decision trees) was trained to predict the continuous Darcy-Weisbach friction factor (f). The surrogate model demonstrated exceptional predictive accuracy on an unseen 20% holdout test set (N = 200), achieving a Coefficient of Determination of R2 = 0.99566 (explaining 99.57% of physical variance), a Mean Absolute Error of 1.487 × 10-4, and a Mean Absolute Percentage Error of 0.819%, with 100% of test predictions strictly bounded within a ±2% error envelope. Gini feature importance decomposition revealed that while macro-scale hydraulics (Re: 71.42%, D: 21.78%) govern global baseline dissipation, microstructural coating dimensions (s: 5.18%, h/s: 1.62%) act as the critical local governing switches determining the drag-reduction margin. The CFD data revealed an optimal drag reduction peak of ηDR,max = +9.253% centered at dimensionless wall spacing s+opt ≈ 16.5 and h/s = 0.55 – 0.65, whereas coarse riblets (s+ > 25) triggered rough-wall vortex penetration penalties down to -24.81%. Crucially, the trained surrogate predicted friction factors in 0.82 milliseconds—achieving an acceleration factor of 4,390,000× (~4.4 million times faster) compared to conventional meshed CFD (3,600 s)—enabling instantaneous 3D response surface exploration. When deployed in continuous industrial transport, the resulting head loss reduction yields electrical savings of up to 14.5 kWh/year per 10 meters of coated pipe, establishing an accurate, ultra-fast computational paradigm for next-generation energy-efficient surface engineering.

item.title: A Workflow for the Systematic Synthesis and Assessment of Trianguleniums as Optical Probes for G-quadruplex DNA Imaging
item.description: Guanine-quadruplexes (G4s), play critical regulatory roles in genomic processes including transcription, replication, and telomere maintenance. Consequently, there is significant interest in understanding G4 dynamics in live cells. One of the approaches to do this is by using optical probes that have distinct fluorescence lifetime upon binding to different nucleic acid topologies. Such probes can then be used in conjunction with Fluorescence Lifetime Imaging Microscopy (FLIM) for sensing and imaging G4s in cells. However, existing probes often suffer from low brightness, poor cellular uptake, or complex synthesis. In this study, we address these limitations by developing a semi-automated workflow for the parallel synthesis and evaluation of a library of fluorescent probes based on the triangulenium scaffold. Utilizing click chemistry, we produced focused libraries of optical probes that allow for biophysical characterization and cellular imaging directly from reaction mixtures, bypassing laborious purification steps and allowing for direct-to-biology (D2B) approaches. This led to the identification of a novel derivative (DM4) with superior photophysical properties compared to benchmark probes. The new probe displays an increase in fluorescence intensity and lifetime upon G4 DNA/RNA binding. Conversely, both its fluorescence intensity and lifetime decreased upon duplex DNA or total RNA binding. These properties combined with good cell permeability and low cytotoxicity, make DM4 an attractive next generation optical probe for G4 DNA imaging via FLIM.

item.title: End-to-End Learning from Experimental Data: Integrating the PC-SAFT Equation of State into Neural Networks Training for Improved Polymer Parameter Estimation
item.description: Accurate and computationally efficient thermodynamic models are essential for the design, optimization, and operation of many (bio)chemical processes involving polymer solutions, blends, and membranes. In this work, we combine machine learning (ML) with the PC-SAFT equation of state (EoS) to predict the non-associating pure component parameters for polymers, enabling the rapid evaluation of the pressure–volume–temperature (PVT) behavior of polymer melts and rubbers. Using a dataset of more than 5,400 PVT measurements for 78 chemically diverse polymers, we systematically evaluate the effects of EoS integration in the training process, the molecular representation, neural network architecture, and transfer learning. A baseline approach trained on pre-fitted PC-SAFT parameters is compared with a physics-informed approach that embeds the EoS in the training loop, enabling endto-end training directly on experimental PVT data. Performance is assessed using 6-fold cross-validation. item.title: An Interpretable Chemoinformatics Benchmark for Evaluating Machine Learning Frameworks, Decoy Sensitivity, and Green Catalyst Prioritization
item.description: As descriptor-based machine learning becomes widely used for reaction yield prediction and catalyst prescreening, controlled validation testbeds with known ground-truth data-generating processes (DGPs) are useful for auditing model behavior, cross-validation protocols, and post-hoc explainability methods. Here we construct and evaluate a synthetic chemoinformatics benchmark of N = 5,000 catalytic alcohol oxidation reactions across 20 independently seeded dataset realizations (100,000 total simulated reactions). By pairing a 22-substrate alcohol library characterized by RDKit exact monoisotopic masses (ExactMolWt) with categorical catalyst and terminal oxidant tiers, continuous thermal profiles, and non-causal synthetic decoy variables (Decoy_Cat_Load, Decoy_Rot_Bonds, Decoy_TPSA), we compare four regression models: Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) Linear Regression, eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost), Random Forest (RF), and Radial Basis Function Support Vector Regression (RBF-SVR).First, we compute the analytical unbounded Gaussian noise floor (3.989% MAE) alongside the 20-seed empirical clamped-oracle benchmark (3.994 ± 0.043% MAE, R² = 0.870 ± 0.003), showing that OLS closely approaches the oracle error floor (4.001 ± 0.044% MAE) under fold-specific standardization. Second, to illustrate how validation splits respond to substrate-level effects, we evaluate a positive-control regime that varies substrate-specific reactivity offsets (σ_sub ∈ {0.0, 4.0, 8.0, 12.0} percentage points), quantifying the divergence between random five-fold cross-validation and substrate-grouped hold-out (GroupKFold). Third, a paired four-model decoy ablation shows that while OLS, XGBoost, and RF exhibit minimal sensitivity to uninformative continuous descriptors (|ΔMAE| ≤ 0.008%, with RF changing by +0.008 ± 0.002%), untuned isotropic RBF-SVR experiences a larger error increase (+0.360 ± 0.026% MAE) consistent with Euclidean distance dilution. Fourth, multi-seed TreeSHAP evaluations show consistent global signal-to-decoy separation across all 20 realizations. Finally, we apply an illustrative multi-criteria Green Performance Index (GPI) to examine the trade-off between thermal activation and environmental penalty in post-hoc reaction ranking.

item.title: Breaking the Trade-Off – Tilted T-Shaped Bis-Heteroaryl Azo Photoswitches with Near-Quantitative Bidirectional Switching
item.description: Azoheteroarenes provide a versatile platform for controlling the molecular geometry and photochemical reactivity of azo switches through heteroaryl substitution. Here, we describe a family of bis-heteroaryl azo photoswitches combining pyrazole with thiophene or selenophene heterocycles, leveraging the independent success of these classes of azo switch. While T-shaped (Z)-isomers are currently only established with a phenyl acceptor motif, single-crystal X-ray diffraction confirms the formation of a T-shaped (Z)-isomer in these new designs where the pyrazole ring acts as the acceptor of a lone-pair–π interaction. Incorporation of pyrazole also substantially improves the bidirectional photoswitching of chalcogen-containing azoarenes by increasing the spectral separation of the (E) and (Z) isomers. These chalcogenophene azo pyrazoles (CAPs) reach up to 99% (Z) under UV/violet irradiation and up to 99% (E) under green light irradiation, while the corresponding selenophene derivatives retain efficient bidirectional switching with more red-shifted excitation. The switches show high resistance to photofatigue, with no significant photodegradation observed over multiple switching cycles. Computational analysis of thermal isomerization further reveals interaction-dependent differences in a coplanar transitionstate geometry, allowing for thermal half-lives of seconds to hours. These results demonstrate that heteroaryl-heteroaryl interactions provide an excellent strategy for controlling both metastable-state geometry and the photochemical performance of azo photoswitches and therefore could underpin the further development and application of advanced photoswitches for a range of light-addressable applications.

item.title: Desalination LLM: Large Language Model Agents Design Efficient Graphene Membranes for Water Desalination
item.description: Graphene nanopores can, in principle, combine high water permeability with strong salt rejection, but finding pore geometries that do both usually requires many molecular dynamics (MD) simulations. We describe a design framework in which a large language model (LLM) grows a nanopore atom by atom, using pretrained predictors of water flux and ion rejection to judge each candidate. Two recent models, Claude Opus 5.5 and GPT-6.1 Sol, were tested with the same prompt and the same design protocol (30 steps, up to 30 trials per step, at most three atoms removed per trial, and a 90% ion-rejection floor). We wanted to know how much of an agent’s performance comes from the model and how much from the surrounding scaffold, so each model was run twice: once as a tool-using agent with access to the predictors, and once in conversation only, where it chose atoms and estimated performance without any feedback. Three scaffold-only baselines that contain no language model were run for comparison. With tools, both models stayed above the rejection floor at every step. Claude Opus 5.5 produced a single, island-free pore with a predicted flux of 122.3 ns−1 at 93.2% rejection, and GPT-6.1 Sol reached 131.7 ns−1 at 90.2%. Without tools the two models erred in opposite directions. Claude Opus 5.5 overestimated rejection and removed too many atoms, ending at 64.3% rejection, whereas GPT-6.1 Sol was overly cautious and recovered only 30% of the flux reached by its scaffold. A greedy search restricted by simple manufacturability rules matched or exceeded both agents in flux. Compared with the MD dataset and the deep reinforcement learning (DRL) designs of earlier work, the agents placed a larger share of their high-rejection pores above 120 ns−1. Taken together, the results indicate that predictor feedback, rather than the language model on its own, is what keeps LLM-guided pore design on target, and the six-condition protocol gives a simple way to make that attribution for other models.

item.title: GPU-accelerated analytic Hartree–Fock gradients
item.description: Analytic nuclear gradients underpin much of computational quantum chemistry, driving geometry optimization and supplying the forces of ab initio molecular dynamics. Yet on graphics processing units (GPUs) the gradient has received far less attention than the selfconsistent field (SCF) procedure it accompanies. In current production codes its construction can cost as much as the entire preceding SCF. Here we present a novel, high-performance GPU implementation of the analytic Hartree–Fock energy gradient. The Coulomb and exchange gradients are evaluated by separate engines to exploit their markedly different sparsity. The exchange gradient retains the full eightfold integral symmetry through an in-kernel ring-buffer compaction that eliminates warp divergence. A hybrid Head-Gordon–Pople/Rys quadrature scheme, translational invariance and GPU-resident shell-pair batch construction further accelerate the evaluation. Benchmarked on NVIDIA H200 GPUs across double-and triple-ζ basis sets against TeraChem, GPU4PySCF, QUICK and VeloxChem, EXESS is the fastest code for every system and basis set tested, with average speedups of 12.2×, 15.4×, 222× and 176× respectively on molecules ranging up to ubiquitin (11,577 basis functions).

item.title: Copper adsorption and release by biodegradable polyester films under field conditions
item.description: In this work we analyze the adsorption of Cu(II) ions on biodegradable mulching films in real conditions by performing a comparison of two commercial PLA/PBAT-based films with a standard olefinic film (LDPE). In particular, in situ tests have been performed at an experimental agriculture center of the Apulian region by miming a real crop cycle. The desorption phenomenon of copper has been also investigated by measuring the amount of metal ions released by the debris of mulching films in the environment at the end of the crop cycle after burying the mulching films under the soil.

item.title: Chemical Filtering of Thymine over Uracil in Prebiotic Hydrothermal Systems: A Mass-Consistent Stochastic Model with Complementary Insights from UV Photodamage Pathways
item.description: The origin of thymine in DNA remains a central puzzle in astrobiology. While Darwinian evolution may have refined RNA into DNA, the initial selection mechanism must have been purely chemical. Here we present UPDSF v6.1.1—the Unified Prebiotic DNA Selection Framework—a mass-conserving, kineticallyconsistent stochastic model of hydrothermal-vent chemistry. At the optimum (90 °C, pH 11, dark vent), a chemical selection index (CSI) of 6.019× emerges through the multiplicative combination of real (direct) T-preferential hydrolysis and pool-composition drift. The model reproduces all key experimental rates (Lindahl, 1993 ; Cleaves et al., 2010 ; Ferris, 1996 ; Sutherland et al., 2020) with explicit provenance tracking and two environmental channels only. UV damage is negligible (<2 % of CSI) under vent conditions. Sensitivity analysis shows that CSI is robust to freemonomer deamination scale and lipid protection, while the 356.96× (~357) fold extrapolated stability ratio (k_U/k_T) is bounded by the activation-energy sweep. The framework is fully stochastic, provenance-tracked, and mass-consistent, providing a rigorous prebiotic pathway from Miller–Orgel monomers to thymine-rich DNA. We further compare our results with the complementary PNAS study of Khosh Abady, Karpourazar & Rentzepis (2026), which demonstrates that UV photodamage pathways act as the dominant evolutionary filter in surface environments. Together, the two mechanisms form a complete two-stage prebiotic model: chemical filtering in the dark (UPDSF) followed by UV selection in the light (PNAS).

item.title: Assessment of machine-learned vs. classical/quantum atomistic simulations for predicting palladium-hydrogen materials
item.description: Palladium-hydrogen materials are used in a wide range of hydrogen storage, purification, sensing, and catalysis technologies; however, accurately predicting the structural and kinetic behavior of palladium hydrides remains computationally challenging. In this work, we present the first systematic assessment of Meta’s Universal Model for Atoms (UMA), a machine-learned interatomic potential, by benchmarking its predictions against density functional theory (DFT) and two widely used embedded-atom method (EAM) potentials for PdHx systems. All approaches were in close agreement for predicting equilibrium structural and thermodynamic properties, such as lattice constants and cohesive energies. In contrast, simulations of nonequilibrium hydrogen diffusion kinetics revealed substantial differences among the methods. Both EAM potentials predicted qualitatively incorrect hydrogen diffusion kinetics, exhibiting nearly instantaneous diffusion dynamics regardless of temperature and failing to capture the formation of molecular H2. UMA correctly reproduced the temperature dependence of hydrogen diffusion and qualitatively matched the DFT-predicted kinetic behavior, although diffusion timescales remained faster than DFT, particularly at lower temperatures. Overall, UMA provides the best balance between predictive accuracy and computational efficiency for large-scale palladium-hydrogen simulations, with DFT serving as a supporting role to obtain more accurate estimates of kinetic timescales, if needed. Our results show that existing EAM potentials (which were historically the most widely used atomistic methods for large-scale studies of these systems) should be used with caution, particularly for palladium-hydride diffusion kinetics.

item.title: Connecting Ligand Structure to Reaction Rate and Coordination Behavior in the Undergraduate Laboratory
item.description: A research-oriented laboratory module has been developed for an upper-division undergraduate inorganic chemistry course with the aim to help students connect ligand structure to reaction rate and coordination behavior. The experiments, which have been implemented and refined at the University of Cincinnati since 2021, focus on the synthesis and characterization of twelve nickel(II) salen-type 10 complexes derived from Schiff-base ligands, which differ by backbone linkers and ring substituents. Over four laboratory sessions, students synthesize and isolate the ligands and nickel complexes and characterize them using analytical techniques including NMR and IR spectroscopy, X-ray crystallography, elemental analysis, and mass spectrometry. In addition to learning the synthetic and analytical techniques, students compare experimental observations and data to investigate how ligand 15 structure affects reaction rate, solubility, coordination geometry, and product formation. Several systems provide particularly useful opportunities to examine unexpected outcomes, including incomplete reactions, solubility issues, and formation of a trinuclear nickel complex from a less rigid ligand. A collaborative data-analysis session allows students to compare results across related ligand systems and develop evidence-based explanations for observed trends and anomalies. Overall, this 20 laboratory provides a framework for incorporating authentic research experiences, collaborative analysis, and problem-solving into undergraduate inorganic chemistry education.

item.title: Catalytic capture of fleeting enamines with palladium electrophiles
item.description: Many reactive intermediates remain chemically inaccessible because they exist only in low equilibrium populations. Although enamines are fundamental nucleophiles in stoichiometric and catalytic reactions, their catalytic use has been largely restricted to systems in which their formation is thermodynamically favoured. Thermodynamically disfavoured enamines exist only transiently and in minute concentrations. Thus, their utilisation requires intermediates with both the stability to capture these fleeting species and the reactivity to drive the subsequent low-barrier bond-forming pathways to completion, thereby preventing the overall reactivity from being governed by the thermodynamics of enamine formation. Here, we demonstrate that low-population enamines can participate efficiently in catalysis through the Lewis-acid-assisted generation of cationic arylpalladium(II) intermediates. This strategy allows a palladium-catalysed α-arylation of acyclic ketones that exhibits broad functional-group tolerance under near-neutral conditions, providing access to transformations that are challenging under conventional conditions. The results of our experimental and theoretical studies support the formation of electrophilically activated cationic palladium intermediates that are responsible for enamine capture and the subsequent formation of carbon–carbon bonds. More broadly, our findings establish a catalytic strategy that involves thermodynamically disfavoured yet chemically valuable intermediates that ordinarily remain latent in equilibrium.

item.title: Replication Units in Time-Resolved Raman Spectroscopy of Cells and Organoids
item.description: Time-resolved Raman spectra of fixed cells can show reproducible spectral differences without establishing independently replicated biological dynamics. We examined what two public archives can and cannot support. In 450 spectra of LLC-MK2 cells exposed to glucose alone or to glucose plus glutamine at nine nominal times, the glucose-only 15- and 30-min arrays were identical in all 30,000 entries. The fine-scale share of temporal contrasts depended on the processing scale: at 90 min, the residual left after 201-channel Savitzky–Golay smoothing amounted to 0.419 of the full contrast norm for glucose and 0.153 for glucose plus glutamine, and both ratios increased monotonically from 101- to 301-channel windows. The two conditions already differed at 0 min by a distance comparable to that at most later times. An invariance argument shows that, without culture or acquisition identifiers, a time-specific shared offset cannot be separated from a systematic condition–time mean. In a hierarchical null simulation with 2,000 realisations per design, a cell-level test rejected a true null in 52.25% of datasets at intracluster correlation 0.3 with two clusters per condition, compared with 2.30% for a test on cluster means. In a neural organoid archive with three traceable culture batches, day-40 minus day-5 contrasts agreed closely between two batches (cosine similarity 0.755–0.980) but not with the third (−0.716 to 0.502) across nine preprocessing settings. Time-resolved Raman studies should report archive integrity, processing-dependent detectability and independently replicated biological change as distinct levels of evidence.

item.title: Methylmercury production across an organic carbon gradient in Fe-rich subarctic soils
item.description: Arctic and subarctic soils accumulate anthropogenic inorganic mercury (Hg) transported from lower latitudes. Under reducing conditions, it can be converted to the neurotoxic methylmercury (MeHg). However, the extent and biogeochemical drivers of MeHg production in these soils remain unclear. Here, we investigated MeHg production in various types of Icelandic soils rich in iron (Fe, 40-110 g kg-1) and presenting varying organic carbon content (OC, 40-250 g kg-1), classified herein as mineral, intermediate or organic soils. Six topsoils (0-25 cm) and three subsoils (70-130 cm) were incubated anoxically for 18 weeks during which MeHg production and release to the aqueous phase were followed together with ancillary parameters (e.g., Fe(III) and sulfate reduction) and microbial community composition. Large MeHg production (up to 11% of total Hg) was observed across topsoils having different characteristics, with topsoils generally exhibiting greater MeHg production than subsoils. A larger release of MeHg to the aqueous phase was observed for mineral soils, indicating a higher potential risk for connected aquatic ecosystems. Total OC content was a poor predictor of MeHg production. In contrast, MeHg concentrations were correlated with (i) the abundance of hgcA, a key gene required for Hg methylation, in a desulfobacterotal group and (ii) geochemical and microbial indicators of both Fe(III) and sulfate reduction. Overall, this study shows that not only organic but also mineral soils are crucial to assess MeHg risks in (sub)arctic environments. Moreover, the extent of MeHg production was better explained by temporal changes in microbial and geochemical processes, including hgcA abundance, Fe(III) and sulfate reduction, than the initial biogeochemical characteristics of the soils.

item.title: Spatiotemporal Decoupling of Antimicrobial and Osteogenic Cues for Tissue Regeneration: Evidence, Design Windows, and a Validation Roadmap
Sequence order controls silver(I) coordination in aqueous His–Met–Pro tripeptide–nitrate mixtures: an ab initio molecular dynamics study
item.description: Silver–peptide interactions underpin peptide-directed synthesis of silver nanomaterials and the silver-resistance machinery of bacteria, yet the molecular-level speciation of Ag(I) in the presence of short peptides and nitrate remains poorly resolved. Here we report 100-ps ab initio molecular dynamics simulations of three sequence isomers of the tripeptide His–Met–Pro (HMP, HPM and PHM; 220 atoms each) in water, with four Ag(I) ions, four nitrate anions and 32 water molecules at 298 K, using the PBE–PAW description (VASP 6.1.0, 500 eV plane-wave cutoff, Γ-point sampling). In all three systems silver remains mononuclear, with average coordination numbers of 2.6–2.9 and only transient Ag–Ag contacts (present in 2–9% of frames at a 3.2 Å cutoff). The composition of the coordination shell is strongly sequence-dependent: His–Met–Pro is dominated by the His imidazole nitrogen (0.48 contacts per Ag) and nitrate oxygen (0.57), whereas His–Pro–Met is dominated by the Met thioether sulfur (0.73) with nitrate largely excluded (0.16); Pro–His–Met shows an intermediate, mixed N/S/nitrate shell and the largest peptide conformational rearrangement (heavy-atom RMSD 6.1 Å, radius of gyration 5.8 Å). Nitrate and water exchange on ∼0.2–1 ps timescales, while peptide N/S donors remain bound for several to tens of picoseconds. These results demonstrate that, at fixed composition, sequence order controls which donors are presented to Ag(I) and therefore the speciation from which silver nanomaterials nucleate.

item.title: Scaffold hopping from deposited crystal pairs: docking-free contact-conservation benchmark and structure-validated method
item.description: Scaffold hopping—replacing a ligand core while retaining function—is almost always scored by two-dimensional similarity to the reference, by docking to a single pose, or by recovery of one literature ligand, while the trivial baseline of copying the reference decorations is rarely reported. We build a benchmark from the Protein Data Bank: 2,886 ligand pairs that bind the same pocket with different Bemis–Murcko scaffolds, across 27 targets and five families, with scaffold- and target-held-out splits. Superposing the two crystal structures and transferring the experimentally solved hop into the reference pocket gives a docking-free contact-conservation criterion: the true hop recovers 80.6% of reference contacts across 40 crystal pairs, and 97% of pairs exceed 0.6; the criterion tracks pharmacophore overlap (ρ = 0.51, n = 50) but not the potency gap (ρ = −0.13), so it measures pose, not affinity. SV-Hop (structure-validated scaffold hopping)—a 60,069-rule core-replacement lexicon, exact graph swap, property/SA/novelty constraints and a learned contact ranker—returns a novel, property-conserved, synthesizable hop for 62.1% of 298 scaffold-held-out references, against 50.3% (property), 44.3% (2D), 27.0% (random) and 0% (copy). The scaffold split holds out scaffolds rather than pockets, so 97.4% of test pairs share a pocket with training; under target shift the gain falls to +5.3 pp (65.3% vs 60.0%) and the ranker transfers weakly (ρ = 0.13). A 388-rule PDB-only lexicon matches coverage and reaches 81.9% on the same target-held-out split, against 65.3% for the full lexicon, and an equal-diversity control attributes part but not all of that gap to candidate diversity. We release the benchmark, lexicon, model and a 22-compound prospective panel.

item.title: LearnM8: A Simple and Modular Molecular Active Learning Framework for any Oracle
item.description: Make-on-demand chemical spaces contain more than 1011 compounds, which makes exhaustive virtual screening by docking or another costly scoring method (the oracle) impractical. Active learning reduces this cost by training a surrogate model (learner) on labeled compounds and using an acquisition strategy to select the next batch to evaluate. However, available implementations are built around particular docking programs and need new code for each oracle, learner and acquisition strategy. Here, we present LearnM8 1.0, an open-source Python package for modular active learning in which the oracle is a replaceable function, such that docking, free-energy calculations, precomputed scores or laboratory measurements can drive the same workflow. LearnM8 provides 19 learners, 7 acquisition strategies and 39 featurizers, together with user-defined cycle schedules, removal of compounds from later cycles that scored worst (pruning), per-cycle diversity metrics, saved per-cycle predictions and a persistent feature cache. In retrospective benchmarks on precomputed docking scores, LearnM8 recovered 98% of the best-scoring 0.1% of compounds in AmpC libraries of 1 to 96 million compounds after evaluating 10% of each library. On a 116-million-compound D4 library the same protocol recovered 91%. In the same study, random selection recovered 9.4% of the 1-millioncompound AmpC library. Smaller batch sizes per cycle improved recovery at higher computational cost, and pruning reduced prediction workload while slightly reducing recovery. LearnM8 is released under the MIT license at https://github.com/drugm8/LearnM8.

item.title: Decoding Ionic Liquid Architecture at the Electrode-Electrolyte Interface in Supercapacitors.
item.description: The increasing demand for efficient energy storage underscores the need to enhance the capacity of electric double-layer capacitors (EDLCs), with electrolyte modification being a promising approach to improve their performance. Ionic liquids offer wide electrochemical stability windows, low volatility, thermal stability, and tunable molecular architectures, making them promising electrolytes for EDLCs. To use the molecular tunability of ionic liquids more effectively, it is important to understand how ion architecture shapes interfacial organization of ions near the electrode and controls charge storage. To understand the integrated geometry and electrostatic organization of ions at the molecular level, here we employ atomistic molecular dynamics simulations to compare imidazolium, pyridinium, pyrrolidinium, and piperidinium-based electrolytes at graphene electrodes to understand how five and six membered aromatic planar and saturated non-planar frameworks organize at the electrode-electrolyte interface and affect the device performance. A common tetrafluoroborate anion, electrode geometry, interelectrode separation, and a fixed surface charge density provide a consistent framework for comparison. Molecular orientation, two-dimensional Voronoi tessellation, ion-density distributions, and charge-screening analyses connect adsorption configurations, lateral packing, and countercharge organization at the interface with capacitance behavior of the individual architectural class. Our simulation results show that Imidazolium exhibits the highest capacitance, accompanied by predominantly surface-parallel rings, while pyridinium exhibits the lowest capacitance and is accompanied by mixed orientations. Our simulation results help establish the structure-orientation-capacitance relationship at the molecular scale, which is essential for designing a future ionic liquid-based electrolyte for high-performance EDLCs for applications such as power buffering in renewable energy systems, peak-power delivery in portable electronics, and industrial energy recovery.

item.title: Stochastic combinatorics with tripeptide dimers: finding the rational outcomes of extended games with structural fluctuations
item.description: While protein- and DNA-based macromolecular systems have previously been used to implement the solutions of certain combinatorial problems, similar progress using small organic molecules has been slow. In this paper, we deploy atomistic simulations to show that the structural fluctuations of the dimers of the tripeptide ProPhePhe (Pro = proline, Phe = phenylalanine) can be used to find the rational outcomes of a special class of extended games. Importantly, the ability of the tripeptides to find rational outcomes is stereochemistry-dependent, with frequencies for finding rational outcomes varying between from around 1 to 17 ns-1 during the course of a trajectory simulation. Overall, ProPhePhe dimer structural fluctuations tend to find the cooperative outcomes of extended games more frequently than self-interested (Nash equilibrium) ones. Our results provide the first example of stochastic combinatorics – the use of stochastic processes to explore the solution spaces of combinatorial problems – using small organic molecules. By demonstrating how complex combinatorial problems can be approached using the structural dynamics of molecular clusters, and suggesting that performance can be tuned through molecular design, this work provides an entirely new direction for research into small-molecule computing.

item.title: Optimising TC/EA–IRMS hydrogen isotope measurements of volcanic glass: H2-amount dependence of δD and application to SIMS calibration
item.description: In TC/EA–IRMS hydrogen isotope (δD) analysis of volcanic glass, sample mass is commonly adjusted according to H2O content so that all samples yield similar H2 amounts, a practice that can obscure any dependence of measured δD on H2 amount. Using a wide-bore reactor with a large graphite crucible that accommodated up to 17 mg of sample and gave an approximately four-fold greater peak area than the standard configuration, we measured two reference materials, IAEA-CH-7 polyethylene (δD = −100.3‰) and an in-house chlorite (δD = −41.1‰), over a wide range of H2 amounts. Measured δD varied linearly with the inverse of H2 amount above 1.5 µmol: the fitted relationship for polyethylene gives δD values about 19‰ higher at 1.5 µmol than the extrapolated value, whereas chlorite showed no resolvable dependence. In six submarine basaltic glasses, the magnitude of the dependence ranged from none to more than twice that of polyethylene and tended to decrease with increasing δD, but polyethylene departed from this trend. Because the dependence differs among samples and is not necessarily cancelled by matching H2 amounts, we determined the δD value of each sample by extrapolation to infinite H2 amount and normalised it with the extrapolated values of the two reference materials. Using the extrapolated values as reference data, normalised SIMS instrumental mass fractionation correlated linearly with anhydrous mole weight across nine basaltic glasses (R2 = 0.84), showing that a composition-dependent matrix correction is required even within basaltic compositions. These results improve both bulk TC/EA–IRMS and in situ SIMS δD analyses and indicate that SIMS datasets calibrated with earlier reference values should be re-evaluated.

item.title: A Multi-Criteria Analytical Framework for the Assignment of Carboxyl-Rich Alicyclic Molecules in Dissolved Organic Matter
item.description: Dissolved organic matter (DOM) is one of Earth’s major organic carbon reservoirs, with most of this pool persisting as recalcitrant DOM (RDOM) over millennia-long timescales. However, the actual molecular structures within this recalcitrant pool remain poorly defined. Carboxyl-rich alicyclic molecules (CRAM) are widely used as molecular proxies for a portion of RDOM, but their assignment commonly relies only on elemental formula boundaries in direct-infusion mass spectrometry (MS) data, which cannot identify structural features or differentiate between isomers with different reactivities. In this work, we used analytical data beyond molecular formulas to more carefully classify CRAM candidates through two complementary pipelines. The pipelines integrated formula-based classification alongside liquid chromatography retention time, tandem MS neutral-losses, and stability tests based on microbial incubations. These pipelines were applied to a case study where DOM was produced from white-rot fungal incubations using small phenolic substrates to represent an idealized terrestrial production of CRAM. When the fungi had access to phenolic compounds alongside glucose, double the number of CRAM candidate features were produced which summed more than five times the total intensity of phenolic compounds alone. Across the different carbon growth conditions, conventional formula-based assignment classified more than 3000 features as CRAM. However, of the 333 CRAM-like features with available tandem MS data, only 41 candidates met the additional analytical criteria from our pipeline. Dissimilarities between these 41 candidates and DOM led to us further refine the fragmentation pattern rules for CRAM assignment, which reduced the candidate pool to just four features. This drastic reduction highlights the need for analytical techniques that can provide structural information during natural DOM sample analysis and simulated environmental testing.

item.title: Late-Stage 4-Methylation of [6,5]-Fused Arenes
item.description: Late-stage methylation of [6,5]-fused bicyclic arenes is a transformation of considerable importance in medicinal chemistry, yet the selective C4-methylation of these privileged scaffolds without directing groups has remained elusive. Here we report a relay strategy for the late-stage 4-methylation of [6,5]-fused arenes that couples temporary C3 iodination with a Catellani-type peri-methylation/ipso-H-termination sequence proceeding through an unusual six-membered palladacycle. A rationally designed thio-cycloolefin ligand bearing an N-acetyl pendant accelerates the peri-C–H activation step while suppressing competing C,C reductive-elimination pathways, thereby enabling selective C4-methylation. Inexpensive trimethyl (or trideuteromethyl) phosphate serves as a bifunctional reagent that delivers both the methyl electrophile and the hydrogen nucleophile, providing convenient access to both CH3- and CD3-labelled products. The protocol accommodates indoles, 7-azaindoles, indolizines, benzothiophenes, and benzofurans, and was applied to the late-stage methylation of drug molecules and to 1 mmol-scale synthesis. Mechanistic studies corroborate the six-membered palladacycle intermediate and identify the hydride source of the ipso-H-termination.

item.title: The liquid-gas equilibrium region for the quantum-volume Bragg-Williams equation of state
item.description: The quantum-volume Bragg-Williams (qv-BW) equation of state, derived from a lattice gas model and a mean-field approximation for the intermolecular interactions, includes a unique temperature dependence theoretically grounded through the connection to the thermal wavelength for particles. Here, the qv-BW equation of state is extended by deriving equations in a semi-analytical approach (one numerical inversion) for the two-phase region describing the liquid-gas equilibrium below the critical temperature. In more detail, equations are derived for the coexistence curve (vapor pressure), the molar volumes of the liquid and gas phases, the vaporization enthalpy, the isochoric heat capacity and the saturation heat capacity. Results are presented for a simple model system with the focus on argon. The results are promising, but limitations in the present model are also revealed. The molar volume of the liquid branch has a minimum contradicting established results, and the result for the vaporization enthalpy is limited by the mean-field approach for interactions. Future prospects are discussed both with respect to method development and applications.

item.title: A neural surrogate for the natural-gas compressibility factor: reference-equation accuracy from synthetic training data alone, benchmarked on 2426 independent laboratory measurements
item.description: The compressibility factor z of natural gas is obtained either from inexpensive empirical correlations or from reference equations of state that require the full molar composition and an iterative density solve. Machine learning has been proposed as a bridge, but almost all published studies are trained and tested on values digitised from the same 1942 chart, so their gains have never been shown on independent laboratory data. We assemble such a test set: 6726 gas-phase measurements from 40 publishedstudiesintheNISTThermoMLarchive,withabsolutepressure,temperatureand composition, from which z follows exactly. On its natural-gas domain (2426 points, 10 laboratories) we evaluate six established methods and a residual neural surrogate trained only on synthetic states fromareferenceequation.Thesurrogateattainsanaverageabsolutedeviationof0.789%, statisticallyindistinguishablefrom AGA8-DETAIL (0.769%) and ahead ofGERG-2008 (0.917%), while reducing the error of the Dranchuk–Abou-Kassem, Hall–Yarborough and Dranchuk–Purvis–Robinson correlations by about 1.1 percentage points at all ten laboratories. Replacing the teaching equation whileholding states,architecture and seed fixed changes testaccuracy from 0.923% to 0.789%: surrogate accuracy is governed by the reference equation chosen to generate its labels. A search over 31 functional families shows that fitted residual corrections transfer for the empirical correlations but not for the reference equations or the surrogate.We also measure the cost such surrogatesassertratherthandemonstrate:thenetworkisslowerperstatethanthereference equation, and fastest only when batched on a graphics processor.

item.title: Assessment of honey samples from Nigerian markets using FTIR spectroscopy and machine learning
item.description: Honey adulteration with cheaper sugars is a concern in Nigerian markets, where conventional tests are slow, costly, and not widely accessible. This study assessed whether Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) spectroscopy combined with machine learning can screen honey for added sugar, and whether such a model can be applied to honey sold in Nigerian markets. A Random Forest classifier was trained on a public FTIR dataset of 16 honeys, each measured pure and with 10, 20, and 40% added sugar. It was compared with PLS-DA, logistic regression, and a support vector machine. Models were tested by leave-one-honey-out cross-validation, so each honey was always predicted by a model that had never seen it. ATR-FTIR spectra were also recorded for 11 honeys purchased from Nigerian markets. Random Forest reached balanced accuracy of 0.70–0.71 and AUC of 0.80–0.87 across three pre-processing methods; Random Forest and PLS-DA together ranged from 0.64 to 0.76 (balanced accuracy) and 0.72 to 0.87 (AUC). Most adulterated spectra were detected, even at 10% added sugar, but about half of the pure honeys were also flagged. The amount of added sugar could not be estimated (RMSECV 12.2 percentage points). The most informative bands lay in the carbohydrate fingerprint region (near 1365, 1031, 902, and 818 cm-1, stable across validation rounds). After ATR and baseline correction, the market honeys closely resembled the training honeys (r = 0.965), but they lay outside the range of spectra the model was trained on, so they could not be classified reliably. A leakage-prone test, with augmentation before a random split, gave 0.87 balanced accuracy, against 0.70 when augmentation was kept inside the training data and each honey was held out, showing how test design can inflate reported results. These results support further evaluation of FTIR with machine learning as a rapid screen, but a local calibration set of Nigerian honeys is needed before market samples can be judged.

item.title: Mixed-Linker Modification of MIL-100(Fe): Structure–Performance Trade-Offs in CO2 Adsorption and Cycling
item.description: Amine groups are often added to metal–organic frameworks to strengthen CO2 binding, usually at a cost in porosity. We examine this trade-off in MIL-100(Fe) prepared by a fluoride-free hydrothermal route, with 5, 10 or 20 mol% of the trimesate linker in the synthesis replaced by the amine-bearing linker 5-aminoisophthalic acid (AIA). Diffraction showed that the MIL-100 framework was retained and spectroscopy detected amine-related groups, although AIA incorporation was not quantified. Increasing AIA content reduced crystallite size from 43 to 18 nm and BET surface area from 1527 to 435 m2 g-1. At 298 K and 1 bar, the modified materials adsorbed 1.3–1.7 mmol g-1 CO2, against 3.1 mmol g-1 for pristine MIL-100(Fe), although the 5 mol% material approached the uptake of pristine MIL-100(Fe) at 14 bar. They also held CO2 less strongly: the isosteric heat of adsorption (Qst), which indicates how strongly CO2 binds, was 16–30 kJ mol-1 at low loading, rising with AIA content, against ~60 kJ mol-1 for pristine MIL-100(Fe). The pristine material also gave the highest predicted CO2/N2 selectivity (~170, against 18–32 for the others, at 298 K and 1 bar). Under flow, however, the ranking changed: in breakthrough tests with 8 vol% CO2 in N2, the 5 mol% material had twice the dynamic CO2 capacity of pristine MIL-100(Fe) (0.20 vs 0.10 mmol g-1), and commercial Basolite F300 the highest (0.46 mmol g-1). Over 40 cycles between 0.15 and 1 bar, uptake reached a steady level and the 5 mol% material kept its crystallinity and surface area (865 vs 861 m2 g-1). No composition was best on every metric: AIA addition reshapes rather than improves CO2 adsorption in MIL-100(Fe), so capacity, binding strength and flow performance must be judged together.

item.title: Analytical nuclear gradients for the CC2 method using pair-natural orbitals based on localized virtual molecular orbitals for excited states
item.description: Analytical nuclear energy gradients are indispensable for optimizing excited-state structures and exploring excited-state potential energy surfaces. Local correlation methods based on pair-natural orbitals (PNOs) have extended correlated wavefunction calculations to large molecules, and their analytical gradients have been developed for ground states but, to our knowledge, not for excited states. In our previous work [M. Hayashi, S. Nagae, M. Saitow, and T. Yanai, J. Chem. Phys. 165, 164118 (2026)], we established the analytical gradient theory of the PNO-based second-order approximate coupled cluster (CC2) method using localized virtual molecular orbitals (LVMOs), which was limited to the ground state. In this work, we report the development of analytical nuclear gradients for singlet and triplet excited states of the LVMObased PNO-CC2 method. Using the ground-state PNOs for all excited states, we inherit the ground-state Lagrangian, including the PNO-construction constraints, and add only excited-state constraints. To reduce the excitation-energy errors arising from the ground-state PNOs, we introduce a PNO truncation correction and develop the gradients including this correction. The formulation is extended to a projected-atomic-orbital-based variant and to the spin-component-scaled scheme. To verify the implementation, we extended our automated symbolic derivation program to spin-orbital algebra and to the excitation vectors of the excited states, and the analytical gradients were validated against selection-fixed finite differences. Using the present method, we accomplished analytical excited-state gradient calculations for real-life molecules with 80–91 atoms.

item.title: Guidelines for minimizing contamination from Ag-based reference electrodes in aqueous and non-aqueous solvents
CelluloseForge: Crystallography-first construction of cellulose systems for molecular simulation
item.description: CelluloseForge is an open-source Python package for reproducibly constructing atomistic crystalline cellulose models. It represents experimental unit-cell data separately from molecular-mechanics parameters and generates unit cells, periodic bulk crystals, chain-parallel slabs for four cellulose allomorphs, and literature-defined 36-chain fibrils. Finite and covalently periodic chains can be parameterized with GLYCAM06j-1 or CHARMM36 and exported as matched GROMACS coordinates and topology. Stable identifiers support reproducible heavy-atom position restraints, while PDBx/mmCIF output and machinereadable build reports support large and auditable systems. Automated crystallographic and topology tests, GROMACS preprocessing, minimization, and short NVT workflows define the validated scope and identify exploratory constructions explicitly.

item.title: An addendum to the chemistry of vicinal hexaketones
item.description: This work adds to previous unpublished and inconclusive works on the synthesis of vicinal hexaketone dihydrates. Based on analytical data, chemical reasoning and DFT calculations, we argue that in the conversion of 2,5-bis-diazo-tetrone-1,3,4,6 moieties to vicinal hexaketones highly symmetrical hexaketone hemiketals were formed. The hemiketal structure will be shown to result from the high energy gain of the dimerization process.

item.title: Soft-drug design for topical JAK1/TYK2 inhibition in atopic dermatitis
item.description: Topical Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitors reduce systemic exposure compared with oral dosing, but they do not eliminate it. Ruxolitinib cream, the current topical benchmark in atopic dermatitis (AD), achieves an Eczema Area and Severity Index 75% improvement (EASI-75) rate of 70.0% at week 8 in TRuE-AD4 and itch relief within 15 minutes, yet its plasma concentrations must still be interpreted against a 281 nM threshold linked in vitro to JAK-mediated myelosuppression. A soft drug — active in skin, designed to be rapidly hydrolysed to an inactive metabolite on entering blood — offers a mechanistically different way to widen that margin, and the approach has been clinically explored with ATI-1777, a topical soft JAK1/3 inhibitor. This study asks what a next candidate would have to look like to be worth making, and how it should be tested before any efficacy claim is entertained. Three analyses were combined. First, a simplified physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) skin–plasma model (1.5% cream, 200 cm2, 12 h, Potts–Guy permeability) compared ruxolitinib, upadacitinib and a hypothetical soft-drug target profile (molecular weight 420, logD 3.2, plasma esterase clearance 300 L/h). Second, 16 known JAK inhibitors with public structures from PubChem were clustered with RDKit using Murcko scaffolds and Morgan fingerprints (Butina clustering, distance cutoff 0.55). Third, five benchmark drugs — ATI-1777, topical brepocitinib, oral soficitinib, tapinarof and ruxolitinib — were compared on published efficacy, plasma exposure and development status, with three commonly repeated figures corrected against primary sources. In the PBPK model the target profile gave a skin partitioning index of 174, about six times that of ruxolitinib (30), and a plasma area under the curve (AUC) of 20 µg·h/L, about one-fourteenth that of ruxolitinib (273 µg·h/L); upadacitinib was intermediate (index 78, AUC 150 µg·h/L). The 16 inhibitors fell into 13 clusters. The pyrrolo[2,3-d]pyrimidine family was the crowded zone, while deucravacitinib (Tanimoto similarity to ruxolitinib 0.10), filgotinib (0.12), upadacitinib (0.18) and peficitinib (0.22) were the most distant chemotypes. The benchmark analysis shows that novelty can no longer rest on the soft-drug idea alone: it must rest on the combination of soft inactivation, a non-crowded scaffold, JAK1/TYK2 selectivity and measured paraoxonase 1 (PON1) clearance that still holds in low-PON1 donors. A five-step validation chain with a pre-specified PON1 gate is proposed. These are paper-validation and ranking results only; they do not demonstrate that any molecule exists, works, or is safe.

item.title: A Chiral Photoactive Ligand for Enantioconvergent Nickel-Catalyzed C(sp2)–C(sp3) Cross-Coupling
item.description: Integrating photochemical catalyst activation and stereochemical control within a single catalyst architecture offers an attractive strategy for asymmetric synthesis. Herein, we report a chiral photoactive nickel catalyst that enables enantioconvergent light-mediated C(sp2)–C(sp3) crosscoupling of an N-Boc-protected pyrrolidine-derived trifluoroborate with (hetero)aryl bromides. The catalyst features a carbazole-decorated biimidazole (biIm) ligand that combines intraligand chargetransfer (ILCT) photoactivity with asymmetric induction, thereby eliminating the need for a separate photocatalyst. The optimized system affords enantioenriched products with high enantioselectivity across a broad range of aryl bromides. Mechanistic investigations provide evidence for stereochemical scrambling through reversible Ni–C bond homolysis, offering a possible pathway for enantioconvergence. These findings establish chiral photoactive ligands as a platform for integrating light-driven catalyst activation and asymmetric cross-coupling catalysis.

item.title: Support Effects in the Catalytic Transfer Hydrogenolysis of Diphenyl Ether over Ru Catalysts
item.description: The selective cleavage of aryl C–O bonds while avoiding hydrogenation of the aromatic ring is a crucial challenge in the reductive valorisation of lignin. Industrial Ru (5 wt%) catalysts supported on wood-derived activated carbon (RuCw) and δ/θ-Al2O3 (RuAl), prepared by deposition–precipitation using Ru recovered from metal-containing waste streams, were compared in diphenyl ether (DPE) hydrogenolysis under catalytic transfer hydrogenolysis (CTH) with 2-propanol and under molecular H2. At 200 °C after 2 h, RuCw gave 92.0% DPE conversion and 63.6% aromatic yield under CTH conditions, compared with 42.8% and 33.4%, respectively, over RuAl. Normalizing apparent rate constants with respect to the Ru accessible by CO chemisorption reduced the activity di]erence to a factor of 1.2-1.4 between 160 and 200 °C, indicating that the accessible Ru population accounts for most of the support-dependent rate di]erence, although uncertainties in CO/Ru adsorption stoichiometry prevent assignment of the residual di]erence to intrinsic kinetics. The corresponding apparent activation energies were found to be 104 ± 7 and 85 ± 5 kJ mol-1. Under CTH conditions, aromatic selectivity followed nearly the same dependence on DPE conversion over both catalysts. At comparable conversion, 2-propanol gave higher aromatic selectivity than molecular H2. Under H2 pressure, dicyclohexyl ether formation was consistent with a greater contribution from DPE ring hydrogenation before C–O cleavage. Under the reaction conditions examined, the support primarily determines the accessible Ru population and hence catalytic activity, whereas the mode of hydrogen supply governs the competition between C–O cleavage and aromatic-ring hydrogenation.

item.title: Orchestrating literature landscaping in drug discovery by coupling citation expansion with large language models
item.description: Systematic literature reviews guide decisions in drug discovery, yet keyword-based retrieval misses relevant work hidden behind synonyms, compound codes and cross-disciplinary vocabulary. Manual screening of large literature pools is slow and costly. Large language models (LLMs) could relieve this bottleneck, but existing tools address either citation-based retrieval or LLM screening, and rarely validate how well the combination performs. We present CESAR (Citation Expansion for Systematic Academic Reviewing), an open-source workflow that assembles domain corpora by following references and citing works through OpenAlex. It screens titles and abstracts with LLMs calibrated against human-annotated reference sets. We demonstrate CESAR on a broad methodological field, total synthesis, and on a narrow drug target, monoacylglycerol lipase (MAGL). For total synthesis, the collected corpus contained 78% of an independently curated reference collection published 2000–2023. The classifier retained 99.3% of those that reached screening, and inexpensive models performed close to the most expensive ones. For MAGL, an open-weight model reduced more than 20,000 records to 893 at no cost, with an estimated 79% of them relevant, while extracting target selectivity, evidence level and compound names in the same step. Run on a single local GPU, the same model matched cloud performance, enabling screening of confidential material without external data transfer. CESAR turns screening of tens of thousands of abstracts into a task of hours to days, at costs from zero to about one US dollar per thousand papers, and keeps expert attention for the decisions that require it.

item.title: Photovoltaic e-waste for PFAS remediation and H2 evolution
item.description: End-of-life photovoltaic modules and persistent fluorinated compounds present distinct challenges for waste management and chemical recovery. Here, we report an integrated approach that uses silicon recovered from discarded photovoltaic modules to promote the mechanochemical defluorination of perand polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS). Subsequent alkaline treatment releases the retained fluorine as fluoride and generates hydrogen through oxidation of the remaining silicon, with SiO2 as a third recoverable product. The recovered fluoride is used to synthesize a sulfonyl fluoride, while the generated hydrogen is employed in heterogeneous catalytic hydrogenations, including reactions catalyzed by palladium supported on recovered photovoltaic silicon. This approach couples the degradation of persistent fluorinated compounds with the recovery of chemical reagents from photovoltaic waste, enabling their subsequent use in organic synthesis.

item.title: Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning Model Implementation for UC Irvine Dataset 322
item.description: The dataset, sourced from the UCI repository, underscores the value of open-source resources in advancing sensor research. In this study, raw sensor data were compressed using polynomial fitting (polyfit), achieving nearly a 100-fold reduction, and subsequently analyzed with the Isolation Forest algorithm to detect anomalies. Python libraries, including scikit-learn, were deployed in an isolated environment to ensure reproducibility and scalability. The workflow was further integrated into Microsoft Copilot, enabling natural language interaction with the AI agent for streamlined big data modeling.

item.title: Pt(II)-Flavin Complexes As Anticancer And Antibacterial Agents
item.description: We report a new chelating pyridyl–imine ligand bearing a riboflavin-derived pendant group and its Pt(II) complexes 1 and 2, designed as cisplatin- and oxaliplatin-like derivatives. Both complexes reacted with DNA and a histone-derived peptide, with 1 showing markedly higher covalent reactivity. However, this trend was not reflected in biological activity. Complex 2 displayed micromolar antiproliferative effects and pronounced antibacterial activity, particularly against Bacillus subtilis, whereas 1 was inactive in the tested models. Cellular accumulation studies excluded enhanced Pt uptake as the origin of this difference. Fluorescence microscopy performed on Escherichia Coli and Bacillus subtilis indicated that 2 affects bacterial DNA and membrane potential, consistent with a dual antibacterial mechanism. Comparison with oxaliplatin and the free flavin ligands showed that both the Pt–oxalate fragment and the riboflavin-containing ligand are required for activity.

item.title: Enantioselective Cobalt-Catalyzed Enyne Cyclo-1,4-Dienylation: Reaction Development and Mechanism
item.description: Cheap-metal-catalyzed asymmetric enyne cycloisomerizations that directly synthesize 1,4-dienes, named here as enyne cyclo-1,4-dienylation (abbreviated as cyclodienylation), remain scarce. The existing methods are largely limited to racemic transformations and mostly for 1,6-enynes. Here, we report a cobalt-catalyzed asymmetric enyne cyclo-1,4-dienylation using both 1,6-enynes and 1,7-enynes, delivering enantioenriched five- and six-membered rings bearing 1,4-diene moieties. The reaction proceeds under mild conditions with an earth-abundant cobalt catalyst and commercially available chiral phosphine ligands, tolerates a broad range of alkyl-, aryl-, and terminal-alkyne substrates as well as carbon-, nitrogen-, and oxygen-tethered enynes, and remains efficient on gram scale with excellent enantioselectivity. Mechanistic experiments and DFT calculations were performed, indicating that the reaction occurs via a pathway involving oxidative cyclometallation, β-H elimination, and reductive elimination. Distortion–interaction analysis was applied to understand the origin of enantioselectivity of the 1,7-enyne cyclodienylation.

item.title: A General Strategy for Active Learning When Predicting Reaction Performance in a Target Domain
item.description: Machine learning models can help guide reaction development, but their usefulness is often limited by the scarcity of training data in the chemical spaces where predictions are most needed. Active learning can reduce this burden by selecting a minimal number of maximally informative experiments. However, standard acquisition strategies such as Bayesian active learning by disagreement (BALD) prioritize uncertainty without regard to the specific prediction domain of interest. Here, we approach active learning for reaction outcome prediction using expected predictive information gain (EPIG), a target-aware acquisition function that scores candidate experiments according to the predictive information they are expected to provide about a specified target distribution. In a Wittig olefination transfer learning task, EPIG adapts a model trained on established reactions compiled from a foundational Wittig textbook to a distinct literature-sourced reaction domain using approximately half as many acquired reactions as BALD. Across 118 retrospective active learning tasks spanning four reaction datasets, four split families, and targets including yield, enantioselectivity, and stereoselectivity, EPIG achieves the strongest early learning performance on the majority of tasks, remains statistically competitive on nearly all tasks, and achieves the greatest reduction in required data relative to established acquisition strategies and baseline methods. These results demonstrate how target-aware active learning can improve the data efficiency of reaction outcome prediction across diverse chemical settings.

item.title: Dual-Microcapsule-Triggered In Situ Polymerization Enables Ultralong Room-Temperature Phosphorescence for Damage Visualization and Dynamic Anti-Counterfeiting
