item.title: All-Dielectric Metasurfaces in Fundamentals, Materials, and Emerging Applications
item.description: The field of optics is undergoing a transformative shift, pushed forward by the demand for miniaturized, lightweight, and highly functional components. Dielectric metasurfaces have emerged as a transformative platform in modern photonics, offering unprecedented control over the amplitude, phase, polarization, and frequency of light within an ultrathin, planar architecture. Unlike their metallic predecessors, all-dielectric metasurfaces exploit Mie resonances, bound states in the continuum, and multipolar interference to achieve low-loss, high-efficiency optical functionalities across the visible, near-infrared, and terahertz spectral ranges. This review covers the field systematically, starting with the common working principles of dielectric metasurfaces and the physical mechanisms that make them so versatile. We then discuss the most widely used material platforms, including their optical properties and practical trade-offs, followed by an overview of the fabrication techniques available today. We look at both traditional top-down methods, such as electron-beam lithography, and emerging high-throughput approaches like nanoimprint lithography and photochemical deposition. We also examine the design strategies and element geometries used to build optical functionality into these surfaces, from simple phase-shifting pillars to more complex resonant architectures. Finally, this review examines the broad range of applications these structures enable, from metalenses and holography to nonlinear optics, biosensing, and terahertz generation. By identifying the key open challenges in fabrication scalability, broadband operation, and active tunability, this review aims to serve both as a reference resource for specialists and as an entry point for researchers from adjacent disciplines, charting a clear roadmap for the next decade of flat-optics research.

item.title: Applicability Domain of Universal Machine Learning Interatomic Potentials at Solid-State Battery Interfaces
item.description: Universal machine learning interatomic potentials (uMLIPs) are trained predominantly on bulk systems, yet are increasingly applied to solid-solid interfaces. Evaluating six uMLIPs against DFT across 24 Li-metal/solid-electrolyte interfaces, we map their applicability domain (AD) and where they break down. Total energies are predicted reasonably well (MAE < 15 meV/atom), whereas interatomic forces at the interfaces are not. Most models underestimate the interfacial formation energy by 0.32 J/m2 and overestimate the work of adhesion by 0.26 J/m2, and none reproduces the stability ordering of polyanion-containing interfaces. Despite large force errors for the interfaces, Li-ion kinetics agree well across models. The errors concentrate on the interface atoms and are larger for the polyanion chemistries. Descriptor-based analysis traces the higher force errors to interfacial environments that lie outside the pretraining data. Fine-tuning can close the accuracy gap, but only with data that samples the bonding across the interface, whereas slab data alone degrades performance. All models struggle on the same chemistries irrespective of the architecture, indicating the coverage of the pretraining data as the primary limitation. Overall, pretrained uMLIPs are suitable for qualitative screening of interfaces with simple single anion electrolytes, while those containing polyanions require interface-specific data.

item.title: Structure – Stability Relationships in Aryl- and Heteroarylmethanesulfonyl Chlorides and Fluorides
item.description: Sulfonyl chlorides are among the most widely used yet least storable building blocks in medicinal chemistry, and arylmethanesulfonyl chlorides in particular remain poorly represented in commercial catalogs because of their limited stability. In this work, the long-term stability of 23 aryl- and 36 heteroarylmethanesulfonyl chlorides and fluorides was evaluated systematically. Decomposition was monitored by 1H NMR spectroscopy in THF-d8 solution at 4 °C and 23 °C for up to 12 months; the solvent was chosen to avoid solvolysis and acidic admixtures, and to minimize water uptake. Whereas at least one batch of each compound remained unchanged in neat form for up to 14 years (median 5.5 years), their stability in solution varied widely, i.e., from complete decomposition of a pyridine derivative within one month to no detectable change over more than 12 months, and was governed by both the electronic nature and the position of the substituent. Notably, both strongly electron-withdrawing and strongly electron-donating substituents proved destabilizing, and the decomposition products differed accordingly: sulfonic acids for electron-poor and benzyl chlorides for electron-rich substrates. Sulfonyl fluorides proved considerably more robust: all heteroaromatic derivatives studied, except isothiazole (8% after 12 months) and pyridine (15% within one week), showed no detectable decomposition over 12 months. We believe that the resulting stability map, which assigns each compound to a defined storage class, will make arylmethanesulfonyl halides practical building blocks for early drug discovery in the near future.

item.title: The Copper(I)-catalyzed Alkyne-azide Cycloaddition “Click” Reaction in Water Requires the Formation of Two Distinct Mononuclear Copper(I) Complexes
item.description: The copper-catalyzed azide-alkyne cycloaddition (CuAAC) has seen widespread adoption amongst numerous fields, but mechanistic details remain elusive and controversial. Using a series of experiments involving fluorogenic coumarin derivatives under pseudo-first order conditions, it was determined that the reaction in conditions close to a physiological environment does not proceed according to the accepted mechanism, but rather requires azide chelation to form a mononuclear copper(I)-azide complex as a preliminary step. Stopped flow studies with a copper-chelating azide further enhanced our understanding of the reaction mechanism, emphasizing the importance of copper-alkyne chelation in which a mononuclear copper(I)-alkyne complex is formed. After both copper(I)-azide and copper(I)-alkyne complexes are formed, they come together to yield the triazole product. This mechanistic proposal of CuAAC in conditions close to a physiological environment is distinct from the currently accepted general model, which proposes dual activation of the alkyne by copper(I) followed by azide interaction. Please note that this manuscript was rejected by several leading chemistry journals for publication in 2015 due to its challenging of existing click chemistry mechanisms. The authors decided to release it to ChemRxiv as a reference for others with a purpose of assisting their experimental designs for bioconjugation.

item.title: Machine Learning for NMR Observables Sensitive to Nuclear Quantum Effects
item.description: Nuclear quantum effects (NQEs) are essential for an accurate description of systems containing light elements. Their omission in classical simulations can lead to significant deviations between theoretical predictions and experimental measurements, particularly for nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) observables that are highly sensitive to quantum nuclear motion. Although NQEs can be treated rigorously by using ab initio path-integral molecular dynamics (AI-PIMD), the substantial computational cost associated with these simulations continues to limit their applicability to large systems and long timescales. To address this limitation, we developed a machine learning-driven PIMD (MLPIMD) workflow for the accurate and efficient prediction of NMR observables, in which NQEs at finite temperature are explicitly included. As a demonstration, we investigate the experimentally measured isotropic chemical shifts, δiso, of the 3He monomer (3He@C706- ) and dimer (3He2@C706- ) endohedral fullerene hexaanions. The resulting predictions show excellent agreement with the experiment and reveal a pronounced influence of NQEs on the 3He chemical shifts in both systems. In particular, NQEs are found to play a key role in determining the chemical-shift difference between the monomer and dimer species. The methodology introduced here is broadly applicable and provides a general framework for investigating NMR observables sensitive to NQEs in complex molecular systems.

item.title: The Evolution of Electronic Structure in Conjugated Molecules Revealed by Mixed-Reference Spin-Flip Time-Dependent Density Functional Theory and Density-Based Analyses: II. Polyacenes
item.description: Large conjugated molecules feature small gaps between occupied and virtual orbital spaces, which results in complex electronic structure patterns in their low-lying states. These orbital near-degeneracies also challenge quantum chemistry methods. Mixed-reference spin-flip TDDFT (MRSF-TDDFT) and density-matrix-based analyses provide useful tools to interrogate electronic structure in large conjugated molecules. This paper investigates one such family—polyacenes. Following our recent study of the ground and low-lying excited states of all-trans polyenes, we track this evolution from benzene to dodecacene using MRSF-TDDFT and densitymatrix-based analyses. In polyacenes, the ground state acquires diradical character as the number of rings increases, while the doubly excited state dominated by the HOMO2 → LUMO2 configuration drops steeply in energy and falls below the La state between nonacene and decacene. MRSF-TDDFT reproduces the experimental La/Lb crossing, which standard linear-response TDDFT misses, and gives singlettriplet gaps close to high-level wave-function benchmarks and singlet-fission energetics consistent with experiment. The analyses show that La remains predominantly singly excited throughout the series and we attribute the strong decrease in its oscillator strength to the growing diradical character of the ground state. The doubly excited state evolves from mixed character in naphthalene, similar to the 2 1Ag− state of the polyenes, to a nearly closed-shell doubly excited state in pentacene and hexacene, and finally to a state with natural orbital occupations resembling those of the ground state in the longest acenes. item.title: Accurate and Rapid Vibrational Spectra of Molecular Crystals from Machine-Learned Interatomic Potentials
item.description: Currently, vibrational spectra of molecular crystals often require computational methods to aid in band assignment, especially in the low-frequency region where no functional group specific transitions exist. DFT methods are the gold-standard for computational spectroscopy, but their high computational cost limits simulations to systems characterized by small unit cells. Universal machine-learned interatomic potentials (MLIPs) offer a much cheaper alternative, but their reliability for phonons in molecular crystals has been little explored. In this work, eleven MLIPs from the ANI, MACE or UMA families of models are tested on geometry optimizations, vibrational frequencies and normal mode character with the same computational workflow utilized by DFT. The resulting phonons are then combined with DFT-calculated IR and Raman intensities to obtain vibrational spectra through a hybrid ML/DFT approach. The method is tested on three dispersion-bound molecular crystals, BTBT, naphthalene and anthracene, and three hydrogen-bonded systems, β-glycine and the two polymorphs of the ethosuximide (ETS) drug. MACE-MH omat, UMA omat and UMA omc emerge as the best-performing models and reproduce the experimental spectra with fidelity comparable to DFT.

item.title: A Doubly Reversible Covalent Adaptable Network for (A)Cellular 3D Manufacturing and Post-Culture Cell Retrieval
item.description: Covalent adaptable networks (CANs) are polymer networks in which bond formation and cleavage occur dynamically and reversibly. They are intensively investigated for 3D cell culture, as they model a more physiologically representative environment than traditional 2D culture. In most 3D matrices, however, cell retrieval for downstream analysis remains limited, and overcoming this limitation would advance in vitro 3D models for biomedical research. Herein, this limitation is addressed by functionalizing a cytocompatible and thermogelling diblock copolymer comprised of poly(2-methyl-2-oxazoline) and thermoresponsive poly(2-n-propyl-2oxazine) with biogenic, dithiolane-bearing lipoic acid. The resulting copolymer (P-LOx) is designed such that crosslinking forms a disulfide-based CAN, which, combined with the thermogelling behavior of the copolymer backbone, yields doubly reversible hydrogels with three key properties: excellent 3D-printability, long-term shape fidelity, and on-demand degradation under mild conditions. P-LOx-based hydrogels are successfully extruded in 3D bioprinting with NIH-3T3 fibroblasts and interleukin 12 reporter HEK293 cells. After crosslinking, cell-laden hydrogels remain stable in long-term 3D cell culture and support inbound-cytokine / outbound-protein diffusion. The limited cell-adhesive properties of the native P-LOx network are improved in hybrid formulations with bioactive additives. Finally, the established cytocompatible decrosslinking protocol enables non-enzymatic cell retrieval with >95% viability and allows downstream analysis, including flow cytometry.

item.title: Mass-Constrained Integration of Cryogenic Propellant Management and Carbon–Hydrogen–Oxygen Resource Recovery for Mars Surface Depots: A Monte Carlo Feasibility Study
item.description: A Mars surface propellant depot must make methane and oxygen, liquefy them and keep them cold on a limited launch mass, and each kilogram of added hardware displaces a kilogram of imported feedstock. This study asks which added layers pay for their mass. Seven nested depot configurations are compared at equal launch masses (9 t, a 30 kW array, 3 t of methane and 10.5 t of oxygen storage) by Monte Carlo simulation of 33 uncertain parameters, with paired comparisons and an independent energy audit. In the reference case (medium heat leak, intermittent power), the baseline holds 5,979 kg of usable propellant after one year and the 2 integrated plant 9,005 kg. Almost all of the gain comes from thermal layers: insulation (+1,533 kg), a vapor-cooled shield (+210 kg) and a cryocooler (+1,138 kg). More equipment does not mean better performance: gas and hydrogen buffers change the delivered propellant by only +22 kg, with a sign that depends on the scenario, a titanium-hydride store lowers it by 44 kg against compressed storage; recycled-material buffers change it by −1.3 kg. Coordinated dispatch adds +122 kg, or +4,547 kg, against a strict-priority baseline. With the parameter support widened two- and threefold, the sign of 7 of ten contrasts is unchanged. Only 5 of the 33 parameters are literature anchored, and the thermal model has no pressure-resolved two-phase tank; thus, the results are screening-level simulation outputs, not measurements.

item.title: Landfill methane recovery and use under deep uncertainty: a satelliteconstrained Monte Carlo decision model for the Norte III landfill, Buenos Aires
item.description: Very large landfills are major methane sources, but site decisions rarely join operator-reported capture, independent emission estimates and the economics of competing gas uses. We built a Latin-hypercube Monte Carlo decision model (300,000 draws, 78 inputs) of landfill-gas generation, collection, surface emission, oxidation, selective covers, biomethane upgrading, additional power generation and photovoltaics, and applied it to the Norte III landfill in Buenos Aires. A bottom-up generation prior is constrained by satellite emission estimates at their own date (2022) and carried to 2025–26. The inferred collection efficiency, 0.13 (0.09 to 0.19) in 2022 and 0.14 (0.10 to 0.21) in 2025–26 (median, 90% interval), follows from the emission, oxidation and reported capture, is conditional on the data and not a measurement, and increases to 0.24 (0.15 to 0.37) with an independent 2025 observation that the model overpredicts by a factor of 3.5. Under no-credit conditions none of eight integrated scenarios has a positive median net present value; wellfield optimization with a selective cover abates methane at a median US$3.6 per tCO2e. Additional engines are profitable in 99% of draws that have surplus gas, but in 69% of all operating states after the planned expansion; biomethane needs US$0.46 per Nm3 (US$14 per MMBtu). A cover helps only if the captured share of blocked gas exceeds an analytic break-even (median 0.14). Conclusions hold under alternative generation histories, satellite scaling and dated Argentine benchmarks.

item.title: Encapsulation of f-block elements in borocarbide cages: Synthesis of a magnetic NdB3C3 clathrate
item.description: We report the synthesis of a boron–carbon clathrate with neodymium guest ions, which is stabilized under high-pressure conditions and recoverable to ambient pressure. The compound, NdB3C3, crystallizes in the bipartite sodalite structure (space group Pm3̄n), as determined by single-crystal X-ray diffraction, and exhibits a zero-pressure bulk modulus K0 = 252(12) GPa. The electronic and magnetic properties of NdB3C3 were investigated using density functional theory with PBE, PBEsol, the HSE06 hybrid exchange–correlation functional, and DFT+U . The screened hybrid and DFT+U computations conducted using the experimental 30 GPa lattice constants of 4.73 Å give a band gap of 0.4 eV with spin-orbit origin and a magnetic ground state where the Nd ions each possess a spin moment of about 3 µB . Without spin-orbit we find no gap. The encapsulation of f-block elements within B–C clathrate cages provides a potential platform for realizing isolated, correlated spins with substantial crystal-field effects, expanding the range of tunable properties for this class of diamond-like materials.

item.title: Active Learning for Fragment-Based Kinase Inhibitor Discovery using Docking
item.description: Drug discovery requires efficient exploration of vast chemical spaces while minimizing computational cost. Fragment-based drug design offers a promising route for generating novel ligands through recombination of fragments, yet the resulting combinatorial search spaces rapidly become too large for exhaustive evaluation. Here, we present an active learning framework for navigating kinase-focused fragment recombination spaces derived from KinFragLib. Our approach combines subpocket-aware fragment recombination, structure-based docking, machine learning surrogate models, and genetic algorithm-inspired exploration through fragment additions, deletions, and substitutions around previously evaluated ligands. Rather than screening a fully enumerated recombination library, the framework iteratively generates and evaluates promising fragment modifications, enabling scalable exploration of large recombination spaces. Using protein kinase A (PKA) as a case study, we evaluate the framework on a recombination space containing approximately 210,000 ligands. Active learning identifies high-scoring candidates while evaluating only about 0.5% of the available ligands with the computationally expensive docking workflow. A greedy acquisition strategy recovers 52% of the global top-50 ligands, substantially outperforming random sampling. In addition, a diversity-aware acquisition strategy increases fragment coverage and exploration of alternative hinge-binding motifs while retaining competitive optimization performance. These results demonstrate that active learning can efficiently navigate fragment recombination spaces and substantially reduce computational screening costs. More broadly, the proposed framework provides a transferable strategy for kinase-focused ligand design and can be extended to other targets when suitable fragment libraries are available.

item.title: AuditRxn: Auditable Fast-Weight Memories for Multi-Step Chemical Reaction Prefix-Prediction
item.description: Multi-step organic synthesis planning requires tracking dynamic molecular transformations, protecting groups, and reaction conditions across sequential chemical stages. Existing chemical language models treat multi-step reaction sequences as flattened token streams within standard autoregressive Transformers. Under this paradigm, context lengths grow quadratically, low-information solvents and auxiliary reagents dilute attention away from reactive transformation centers, and hidden state transitions remain uninterpretable black boxes that hallucinate physically impossible steps violating valence rules and stoichiometric conservation. In this work, we propose AuditRxn, an auditable fast-weight memory framework for multi-step chemical reaction prefix-prediction and synthetic pathway planning. AuditRxn introduces a Chemical Fast-Weight Memory (CFWM) that dynamically binds reacting functional groups and catalytic states into a recurrent associative matrix state via an online Hebbian update rule, achieving 𝑂 (1) recurrent step complexity. To guarantee physical validity, a Constraint- Audited Recurrent Alignment (CARA) module inspects memory readouts against hard chemical constraints—including atomic valence, stoichiometric mass balance, and solvent-reagent hazard compatibility—projecting unconstrained latent trajectories onto an admissible reaction manifold while issuing step-wise audit certificates. Furthermore, Counterfactual Prefix-Aware Calibration (CPAC) trains the memory dynamics against perturbed reaction prefixes to suppress error cascades in autonomous multi-step rollouts. Comprehensive evaluations across four benchmark datasets demonstrate the superiority of AuditRxn: on USPTO-50K retrosynthesis, AuditRxn attains a Top-1 accuracy of 51.82% (+1.87% over competitive baselines) with 99.92% chemical validity; on SMolInstruct forward synthesis, it reaches 66.8% Top-1 exact match; on USPTO- Condition, it achieves 0.2985 overall condition accuracy; and on PaRoutes multi-step route planning, it improves Solve@10 route completion to 75.4% while reducing 10-step trajectory inference latency by 62.3%.

item.title: Sharp Bounds for Raman Band-Area Ratios
item.description: Nonnegative signal and background components, bounded observational error, constraints on background smoothness and band-free anchor measurements define a set of admissible decompositions. Linear-fractional optimization gives the exact minimum and maximum band ratios over this set, while a feasibility problem tests consistency of the imposed constraints. A closed-form bound relates remaining area uncertainty to the anchor spacing, background curvature, noise and band profile. In a study of 320 simulated spectra, the computed intervals contained the known ratios whenever the imposed assumptions were satisfied. Across 3,282 additional simulated configurations, the analytical bound was respected; its finite values were con-servative. Under bounded-noise simulations, restricted central integration windows improved identification for the investigated profiles, particularly for Lorentzian bands; on measured backgrounds, this advantage appeared only at high signal-to-noise ratio. In a semi-synthetic study using 70 measured sulfate-only spectra, leave-one-concentration-out calibration produced intervals containing the known ratios in all 2,520 evaluated window and sensitivity configurations. However, precise identification was often unavailable despite close agreement among six conventional baseline-correction settings. Application to measured nitrate–nitrite mixtures was further complicated by nitrate-band overlap, and the available calibration constraints did not identify the corrected ratios tightly. These results distinguish numerical agreement among baseline estimates from identification supported by explicitly defined spectral assumptions.

item.title: Sliding Window Attention with Auditable Chemical Sinks for Long-Sequence Molecular Transformation Modeling
item.description: Long molecular transformation sequences require models to track local bond changes and persistent reaction constraints. Conventional Transformers face high context costs, diluted attention, and chemically invalid predictions. We propose ChemSWA, an efficient and auditable framework for multi-step synthesis modeling. Adaptive Chemical Sliding Window Attention combines local windows with persistent attention sinks to retain reaction states at 𝑂 (𝑊 · 𝐿) computational complexity. A constraint-audited attribution mechanism checks chemical conservation and produces step-wise certificates, while counterfactual calibration reduces error accumulation during rollout. On USPTO-50K, ChemSWA achieves 52.14% Top-1 accuracy and 99.95% chemical validity; it reaches 92.85% Top-1 accuracy on USPTO-MIT. On PaRoutes, it achieves 76.10% Solve@10 with 3.85 s average expansion latency, and on USPTO-Condition it reaches 0.3015 multi-slot accuracy.

item.title: Dynamic changes in hydrogen evolution catalysis impose an upper bound on electrochemical hydrogen storage in Pd
item.description: Efficient storage of renewably produced hydrogen remains a serious bottleneck in the global transition to a hydrogen-based energy system. Production of metal “super- hydrides” with a greater than 1:1 metal to hydrogen stoichiometry, produced by an electrochemical driving force in aqueous electrolyte, is experiencing emerging interest as a possible solution to this critical challenge. In this work, using palladium and its hydride (PdHx) as a model system, we combine state-of-the-art grand canonical density functional theory (DFT) and operando X-ray diffraction to investigate the feasibility and limitations of electrochemical hydrogen storage via formation of metal hydrides. We develop a unique computational model of PdHx with high granularity, particularly in the high loading (0.6 <x ≤1.0) regime. After benchmarking calculated lattice strain to operando X-ray diffraction measurements, we reveal that there is a signifi- cant energetic penalty to filling all six octahedral sites surrounding Pd, and that the well-known α−/β−PdHx coexistence is a macroscopic phenomenon. Using our com- putational model of PdHx, we calculate the bias-, coverage-, and loading-dependent activation barriers and reaction energies for the Volmer and Tafel reactions. Our find- ings reveal that dynamic changes in the activation barriers and reaction energies of hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) sub-reactions impose an upper bound on electro- chemical hydrogen storage, well below theoretically predicted loadings via formation of superhydrides. This work establishes a formalism for theoretical investigations of the electrochemical formation of metal hydrides, and provides fundamental insights into the critical importance of the surface in electrochemical loading of metal hydrides.

item.title: Isocyanide Ligand Tuning of Rhenium Imido N−H BDFE Values for Catalytic Dinitrogen Reduction
item.description: During N2 reduction cycles that involve transition-metal-mediated N2 splitting to nitrides, it is often thermodynamically difficult to form the first N–H bond on the way to ammonia. Increasing this N–H bond dissociation free energy (BDFE) is challenging because changes in the pKa and redox potential typically counteract one another. Here, we report that pincer-ligated rhenium complexes containing isocyanide ligands have dramatically higher imido N–H BDFE values than analogous chloride, cyanide, and pyridine complexes. Systematic electronic and steric variation of the isocyanides revealed that the ReV/IV reduction potentials for the nitride complexes can be varied over a range of ca. 2 V with more muted changes in the ReIVN–H pKa values, resulting in large N–H BDFE values that can be tuned over a range of 16 kcal/mol. Using this strategy, several new Re catalysts for N2 reduction to NH3 were discovered, including an alkyl isocyanide complex that produced up to 22 equiv of ammonia per Re center at room temperature using SmI2 as reductant and ethylene glycol as a proton source. The results provide guidance on ligand tuning for forming N–H bonds from nitrides as part of homogeneous catalytic cycles for conversion of N2 to NH3.

item.title: Copper-Catalyzed Enantioconvergent Synthesis of Sulfoxides from Racemic Sulfinate Esters and Organoboronic Acids
item.description: Chiral sulfoxides are important structural motifs in drug discovery and asymmetric synthesis. Transition-metalcatalyzed approaches to their enantioselective preparation have largely relied on thioether oxidation or coupling reactions involving highly reactive nucleophilic sulfinyl donors, such as sulfenic acids and sulfenate anions. Here, we report a copper-catalyzed enantioconvergent coupling of racemic sulfinate esters with organoboronic acids, in which the sulfinate esters serve as electrophilic sulfinyl donors. This method provides access to highly enantioenriched sulfoxides bearing two minimally differentiated aryl substituents, which are challenging targets for conventional asymmetric oxidation. The reaction also accommodates alkenylboronic acids and exhibits broad functional group tolerance, offering a complementary route for the catalytic asymmetric synthesis of sulfoxides from readily accessible starting materials.

item.title: Nucleophile-Stabilized Transient o-Quinodimethide Forges a Common Gateway Toward C-1 P/N/O/C-Substituted Tetrahydroisoquinolines
item.description: C-1-substituted tetrahydroisoquinolines (THIQs) represent a highly valuable and biologically privileged class of nitrogen heterocycles, owing to their stereochemically rich, structurally versatile scaffolds and widespread presence in medicinally relevant compounds, natural products, and bioactive molecules. Their remarkable pharmacological diversity and tunable molecular architecture make C-1-functionalized THIQs particularly powerful platforms for the discovery, design, and optimization of therapeutically important molecules. Despite their considerable significance, a general and versatile strategy for accessing structurally diverse C-1-functionalized THIQs remains highly desirable. Herein, we report a unified yet remarkably versatile method for the synthesis of C-1 P/N/O/C-functionalized THIQs, providing direct access to structural motifs reminiscent of the cores of six distinct C-1-substituted pharmaceutically and biologically relevant scaffolds. In particular, we have provided convenient access to the cores of IBR-2 (RAD51 inhibitor) and Eudistomin U (alkaloid), and a precursor of Praziquantel (marketed anthelmintic drug). The transformation proceeds from readily accessible 2-alkenylaldimines and a broad range of nucleophiles, including NH-amides, NH-heterocycles, dialkyl phosphites, and C-nucleophilic indoles, under mildly basic conditions. Notably, the method can be further extended to the selective synthesis of C-1-alkylated and C-1-oxygenated THIQs through the use of primary and secondary nitroalkanes, respectively. The reaction exhibits an exceptionally broad substrate scope, excellent functional-group compatibility, and operational simplicity, while readily enabling synthesis on a multi-gram scale, underscoring its practical potential for the preparation of medicinally relevant THIQ architectures. Mechanistic investigations reveal that the reaction proceeds through the generation of azabicyclo-o-quinodimethide (ABQ) interme-diates via thermal 6π-aza-electrocyclization of 2-alkenylaldimines. Competition experiments involving nucleophiles and Diels-Alder dienophiles, reactivity studies with a discrete iminium intermediate, control experiments, isotopic labelling and kinetic analyses using real-time 31P NMR collectively uncover an intriguing interplay between the nucleophile (NuH) and the ABQ intermediate. These studies support the transient formation of an ABQ•NuH complex, which subsequently undergoes basepromoted nucleophilic 1,4-addition to furnish the corresponding C-1-functionalized THIQ products.

item.title: POLEN: An OpenMM Framework for ML/MM Simulations with Mutually Polarizable AMOEBA Embedding
item.description: Hybrid machine-learning and molecular mechanics formulations have been growing over the years. The attractive cost-effectiveness for big systems (such as protein complexes) has made these methods gain attention in the computational chemistry/biology field. In these theories, one of the most discussed themes is embedding, which can add or remove physics from the system. Here, we present POLEN (POLarizable Embedding for Neural-network potentials), an OpenMM plugin for ML/MM simulations with a mutually polarizable AMOEBA embedding, including a variant whose ML-trained head (MuPE(ML)) predicts multipoles, polarizabilities, and charge penetration at each simulation step. We tested it on three systems: a push-pull chromophore which a strong solvatochromic shift (p-nitroaniline in water); a protease-inhibitor complex with a buried salt bridge (trypsin-benzamidinium); and a kinase-inhibitor complex with a halogen bond (CK2α–TBB−).

item.title: Crystallographic Continuity Enables Programmable Living Biointerfaces
item.description: Dynamic biological entities are versatile but remain vulnerable to immune clearance, premature chemical exchange, and environmental degradation. Metal–organic frameworks (MOFs) offer porous matrices for bioencapsulation; however, standard polycrystalline or nanoparticulate shells contain structural defects that compromise protective performance and molecular selectivity. Here, we demonstrate the complete encapsulation of viruses, bacteria, and mammalian erythrocytes within continuous single-crystalline ZIF-90 via biocompatible aqueous routes. Interfacial electrostatics and coordination kinetics shift the nucleation-growth balance to favor particle coalescence and crystallographic fusion at the biological surface. Unlike conventional nanoparticulate ZIF-8 coatings, continuous ZIF-90 single crystals restrict molecular access, shielding host bacteria from ultraviolet radiation and antibiotic stress while preventing premature immunostimulatory signaling. Under acidic conditions mimicking the tumor microenvironment, ZIF-90 degrades, releasing active Escherichia coli and exposing intracellular bacterial triggers. In vivo, these biohybrids induce pyroptotic cell death and suppress pulmonary metastasis. Crystallographic continuity thus provides a structural basis for coupling biological shielding with environment-responsive activation, establishing a physical foundation for programmable biointerfaces.

item.title: Ipso-selective pyridine-to-aniline editing through amine-induced fragmentation
item.description: Skeletal editing enables the remodeling of aromatic frameworks, but pyridine-to-aniline conversions can generate multiple positional isomers, complicating analogue synthesis. Here we report an ipso-selective strategy that separates regiochemical control from diversification of the aniline nitrogen. Pyridines are converted through dearomatization and cycloaddition into stable, isolable bicyclic ketones, which undergo amine-induced condensation–fragmentation to afford anilines with the amino group positioned at the site corresponding to the original pyridine nitrogen. Both primary and secondary amines participate, enabling divergent synthesis from a common intermediate. Notably, regioisomeric intermediates derived from a 3-substituted pyridine converge to a single aniline product. The method also enables preparation of multiple analogues from a tropicamide-derived scaffold, illustrating the potential of this modular approach for medicinal-chemistry scaffold diversification.

item.title: Polymer Informatics in the Era of Foundation Models: From Representation to Autonomous Design
item.description: Foundation models, pretrained on broad datasets and adapted to multiple tasks, offer a way to reuse chemical knowledge across polymer property prediction and inverse design. Realizing this opportunity requires connecting learned representations to materials whose properties also depend on molecular populations, formulation, processing, and measurement conditions. Here, we review advances in polymer foundation models and the data, representations, and experimental workflows that support their use in materials design. We organize these developments around the polymer material state, a description linking chemical identity to molecular distributions, architecture, morphology, and preparation history relevant to a target property. This perspective relates the material described by a model or simulation to the specimen prepared and measured experimentally. We examine what polymer models learn during pretraining and adaptation, how polymer representations retain relevant material information, and how predictions can guide experimental choices. The discussion follows candidate polymers through synthesis, processing, and prospective experimental validation to consider how experimental feedback can improve both models and the preparation of materials for specific applications. We also discuss how foundation models could help connect candidate selection with automated experiments, and the practical requirements for reliable and more autonomous polymer design. Our aim is to clarify how progress in foundation models can meet the practical needs of polymer research and support closer connections between computational polymer design and experimental discovery.

item.title: A reactor concept for more sustainable chemical vapor deposition of hard coatings
item.description: Chemical vapor deposition (CVD) is a key technology for producing hard coatings on cutting tools, but its sustainability is challenged by high energy consumption and low precursor utilization. We present a novel reactor concept for hard coating CVD inspired by spatial atomic layer deposition, aiming to reduce environmental impacts through minimized reactor volume, reduced thermal mass, and the possibility for precursor recirculation. The concept is based on a small modular inline reactor in where the substrates are coated with TiN, as a model system, by rotating between areas with TiCl4 and NH3 exposure, allowing separation of the precursors in the different gas outlets. Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulations were used to optimize gas flow management and life cycle assessment (LCA) was used to compare the proposed design with a conventional industrial batch CVD reactor for TiN-coated cutting inserts. The analysis indicates reductions of approximately 40% in global warming potential and 50% in fossil resource scarcity without precursor recycling. Assuming recovery of 50% of TiCl4 and 80% of NH3, the environmental impacts were further reduced to approximately 36% and 23% of those of a conventional process for global warming and fossil resource scarcity, respectively.

item.title: Structural Analysis of HRF-4467, a Potent Second-Generation HIV-1 Maturation Inhibitor
item.description: HRF-4467 is a betulinic acid-derived HIV-1 maturation inhibitor that targets the canonical CA-SP1 region and blocks the final proteolytic step of viral maturation. Here, we characterize HRF-4467 and its para-fluoro analog using solution and solid-state NMR spectroscopy, supported by quantum-mechanical calculations. Using this approach, we established the molecular connectivity and conformation of HRF-4467 in solution and in the solid state. Introducing a para-fluorine substitution produces localized changes within the aromatic moiety without substantially altering the rest of the molecular scaffold. This work establishes the para-fluoro derivative as a structurally representative analog of HRF-4467 and highlights 19F NMR spectroscopy as a powerful tool for directly investigating inhibitor conformation and molecular recognition within the HIV-1 capsid maturation intermediate assemblies.

item.title: Electrosynthesis of Free-Standing Polyoxometalate–PEDOT Hybrid Thin Films at a Polarizable Liquid|Liquid Interface
item.description: Polyoxometalates (POMs) are versatile molecular redox systems, yet their electrochemical behavior at polarizable liquid|liquid interfaces remains unexplored. Here, we investigate Keggin-type phosphomolybdic acid (PMA) and phosphotungstic acid (PTA) at a polarizable aqueous|α,α,α-trifluorotoluene interface and demonstrate their use as molecular oxidants and dopants for the interfacial electrosynthesis of free-standing POM-poly(3,4-ethylenedioxythiophene) (PEDOT) hybrid thin films. Voltammetry and in situ spectroscopy reveal potential-dependent adsorption and accumulation of POM anions at the interface. Under controlled interfacial polarization, accumulated POMs generate a highly acidic nanoscale reaction environment and catalyze the initial C−C coupling steps of EDOT oligomerization, enabling POM-PEDOT film formation despite thermodynamically unfavorable direct electron transfer between EDOT and the POMs. The resulting PEDOT nuclei evolve into conductive films that sustain growth through a redox cycle in which the POMs act as terminal oxidants and dopant anions. Mixing PMA and PTA markedly enhances growth kinetics, yielding robust, transferable hybrid films with hierarchical three-dimensional morphologies, high POM loadings, and preserved Keggin structures. Ex situ electrochemical characterization reveals the coexistence of PEDOT charging and highly reversible POM-centered redox processes, producing capacitances of up to 48 F g–1 in organic electrolyte and >90% capacitance retention at scan rates up to 1 V s–1. Tyrosine–silver interactions: Comparing [Tyr,H]+ and [Tyr,Ag]+ using mass spectrometry, UVPD, and IRMPD action spectroscopy
item.description: Metal complexes of peptides and proteins are central to biological systems and to the synthesis of functional subnanometer biomaterial templates, such as silver nanoclusters (NCs). Although tyrosine (Tyr) is widely recognised as an effective reducing and stabilising agent in silver nanoparticle production, its fundamental interaction with an isolated silver cation remains poorly understood. Here, we present a joint experimental and theoretical investigation of the structural and optical properties of the mass-selected [Tyr,Ag]+ complex, using [Tyr,H]+ as a structural benchmark. We introduce a new experimental platform that, for the first time, combines a benchtop continuouswave (cw) mid-infrared (MIR) laser and a tunable ultraviolet (UV) optical parametric oscillator (OPO) in a single iontrap setup. Action spectra were recorded in both the mid-IR (1134–1938 cm−1) and UV (234–390 nm) spectral regions. Because [Tyr,Ag]+ exhibits a low propensity for fragmentation, mid-IR photodissociation was achieved by attaching a weakly bound H2O tag. The experimental infrared multiphoton dissociation (IRMPD) and ultraviolet photodissociation (UVPD) spectra were combined with quantum-chemical simulations to identify low-energy conformers and assign their vibrational and electronic transitions. This complementary approach fingerprints the structural and electronic motifs associated with Ag+ binding. The UVPD spectra provide clear evidence of chargetransfer excitations between the aromatic ring of tyrosine and the silver cation. These results provide molecularlevel insight into the early stages of silver–biomolecule coordination.

item.title: Lost in Chemical Space: Local Open-Source Large Language Models Display Model-Dependent Adherence to Reference Data in Molecular Generation
item.description: Large language models (LLMs) can generate drug-like molecules and may be used locally in drug discovery projects where confidentiality and intellectual-property constraints preclude the use of external APIs. Weight quantization enables deployment of large open-source LLMs on limited hardware, but its impact on molecular generation and on the ability of models to follow reference chemical spaces remains poorly understood. Here, we evaluated Gemma-4-31B, GPT-OSS-120B, Mistral-Small-4-119B, and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B at the BF16 (original precision), Q8, Q6, and Q4 quantization levels in two molecular generation tasks. The models were prompted either to generate small molecules without constraints or to generate drug-like molecules conditioned on 69 reference kinase inhibitors provided in-context. Quantization increased inference throughput in a model-dependent manner, with the largest gains, up to 24-fold increase in performance, occurring for Gemma-4-31B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B. In the task of unconstrained generation, model quantization did not affect molecular validity, uniqueness, drug-likeness, diversity and synthesizability. In the task of reference-guided generation, however, the models displayed markedly different levels of adherence to the provided chemical space. Gemma-4-31B was the only model that consistently generated small molecules similar to the reference compounds at all precision levels. Mistral-Small-4-119B and Qwen-3.6-35B-A3B failed to generate small molecules according to the reference chemical space. GPT-OSS-120B showed adherence to the reference molecules at BF16, Q8, and Q6, but lost the capacity to generate molecules in the desired chemical space at the Q4 quantization level. These results show that quantization can substantially improve the performance of local LLMs for molecular generation without compromising output quality, although model selection and validation is essential for guided exploration of the chemical space.

item.title: Hetero-Diels-Alder Reaction of Alkenes and Electrochemically- Generated o-Quinonediimines
item.description: Electrochemically driven organic transformations have emerged as a versatile approach for developing more sustainable synthetic methods, offering precise control over redox processes while replacing stoichiometric oxidants with electricity. In this context, an efficient electrochemical strategy for the generation of highly reactive o-quinonediimines from readily available o-phenylenediamines is reported. Anodic oxidation enables their in-situ formation and subsequent cycloaddition with diverse alkenes, affording valuable tetrahydroquinoxaline cycloadducts in good to excellent yields. The broad substrate scope, together with the successful derivatization of the products, highlights the synthetic utility of this approach.

item.title: 3D Structure Analysis from XAS using Diffusion Models
item.description: The local three-dimensional (3D) atomic structure of materials and molecules can be interrogated by X-ray absorption near-edge structure (XANES), a powerful analytical technique. Here, we introduce a diffusionmodel-based approach that rapidly infers candidate 3D structures from X-ray absorption spectroscopy (XAS) data. The method is validated on multi-element hard X-ray XAS datasets and generalizes across a broad range of molecular and material systems without imposing restrictions on the number of constituent element types. Compared with multi-round iterative optimization methods for 3D structure determination that use a structure-to-spectrum model as the core spectral calculation engine, our approach substantially improves data analysis efficiency, enabling 3D structure determination within a few reverse diffusion steps. On low-end consumer GPUs, 3D structure analysis takes 0.5–5s. We anticipate that this method will significantly facilitate online data analysis at beamlines and associated real-time experimental planning and optimization, enable batch screening of atomic-level 3D structures, and improve the efficiency of conventional 3D structure fitting.

item.title: AI Agents as supporting infrastructure for all-solid-state battery development
item.description: Materials discovery increasingly depends on a multiscale ecosystem of simulations, experiments, and shared facilities, yet advances in individual AI tools do not by themselves connect the decisions that link these components. This gap is especially severe in all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs), whose development couples electrochemical performance to interfacial stability, mechanics, processing, manufacturability, reliability, safety, and cost. Here we argue that AI agents could support ASSB development toward commercial viability by maintaining a shared decision–evidence state that links materials discovery and optimization to cell-level validation and manufacturing constraints. We develop this argument through three complementary dimensions of scientific agency: coordination across heterogeneous resources, method augmentation across models and scales, and project-level adaptation over time. Cross-domain demonstrations establish several relevant capability primitives, including stateful tool planning, task execution, and delegated analysis. Agents should therefore be evaluated as supporting infrastructure for concurrent ASSB engineering rather than as autonomous replacements for scientific expertise. Their value ultimately lies in driving materials development in the context of interfaces, cell architectures, and manufacturing processes toward the performance, reliability, safety, and cost requirements of ASSB commercialization. context & scale Commercializing all-solid-state batteries (ASSBs) requires more than identifying high-performing materials: ion transport, interphase chemistry, mechanics, processing, cell architecture, reliability, safety, and cost impose coupled constraints that can invalidate otherwise promising candidates. This Perspective argues that AI agents could serve as auditable infrastructure, maintaining a decision-evidence state that connects objectives, specimen histories, models, uncertainties, actions, and validation to support ASSB development. Such infrastructure could broaden research across instruments and engineering stages, strengthen validation by linking atomistic, mesoscale, continuum, and experimental descriptions, and preserve evidence and revisions throughout development cycles. Future efforts should move beyond task-level demonstrations toward systematic ASSB development, establishing whether agents can contribute to the development of reliable and economically viable ASSB systems.

item.title: Order-Disorder Phase Transitions and Site Occupancy Pattern in Fe1.5Ni1.5Ga4 Unravelled by Resonant Scattering
item.description: The insufficient X-ray scattering contrast and similar neutron scattering cross-sections of Fe and Ni render the accurate determination of ‘coloring scheme’ ambiguous in the vacancy ordered 43 −superstructure of CsCl-related phase Fe1.5Ni1.5Ga4. Therefore, to overcome this limitation, X-ray resonance diffraction near the K-absorption edge of Fe has been utilized for the accurate site occupancy pattern of Fe and Ni in the structure of Fe1.5Ni1.5Ga4. Measurements on three independently annealed samples with progressively longer annealing times revealed no evidence of atomic ordering, instead, Fe prefers to partially occupy the Ni site (48𝑔 Wyckoff site) in the structure of binary Ni3Ga4 (𝐼𝑎3̅𝑑 space group, 𝑎 =11.52 Å). The vacancy ordering present at the 16𝑏 site drives the lattice distortion in the structure. Upon heating to ~955 K, the room-temperature (RT) structure transforms to the 2.9 Å CsCl-type structure (𝑃𝑚3̅𝑚 space group), where Fe, Ni and vacancy are randomly distributed suppressing the lattice distortions. DFT based calculations on the hypothetical ordered model predict a ferromagnetic ground state with non-magnetic and antiferromagnetic states lying very close to it in energy. This near-degeneracy points to a highly complex magnetic energy landscape with competing ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic interactions, which explains the experimentally observed spin-glass behavior.

item.title: A Scoping Review of Diffusion-Based De Novo Molecular Generation: Architectures, Evaluation, and Open Challenges for Computational Drug Discovery
item.description: Diffusion models form the bulk of generative frameworks used in de novo molecular design, yet the literature remains fragmented across model formulations, molecular representations, and generative tasks, and inadequate systematic accounts exist of how these models are steered towards molecules with desired properties, an aspect of drug discovery that is paramount to acceptance. We present a scoping review of diffusion-based neural networks applied in de novo drug discovery between 2020 and 2026. Following the PRISMA-ScR (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses extension for Scoping Reviews) protocol, we categorise the literature into non-mutually exclusive themes covering methodological contributions, conditioning mechanisms, molecular representations, symmetries, and multi-modal integrations, and outline the datasets and evaluation metrics used throughout. Three findings emerge. First, diffusion did not displace earlier architectures so much as absorb them: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs), Autoencoders, and Transformers persist as backbones, and what changed was the training objective. Second, conditioning strategies reduce to structural anchoring, target-aware biochemical conditioning, property-driven steering, and multimodal latent conditioning; within these, the point in the reverse trajectory at which a conditioning signal is applied is a design variable distinct from the signal itself. Third, evaluation remains unstandardised across frameworks, datasets, and definitions. We identify the resulting gaps in controllability and interpretability as the central open challenge for conditioned molecular generation and outline the direction to ease them as this would enable generation of molecules that match the preferred property profiles.

item.title: Facile Nitrogen Doping of Electrospun Mesoporous Carbon Nanofibers via Urea Addition for Polysulfide-Confining Li-S Cathodes and Interlayers
item.description: Lithium-sulfur (Li-S) batteries offer high theoretical capacity, but polysulfide dissolution and shuttling cause rapid capacity fade. Nitrogen functional groups can anchor polysulfides, yet in our previous work, introducing them through a post-carbonization cyclized-PAN treatment sacrificed much of the carbon nanofiber (CNF) mesoporosity, and Nfunctionalizing both cathode and interlayer performed worst. Here, nitrogen is introduced during fiber formation by adding urea to a PAN/PMMA precursor before gas-assisted electrospinning, followed by stabilization, carbonization, and CO2 activation. This gives N-doped mesoporous CNFs with better control over the balance between nitrogen content and pore structure. Across four cathode/interlayer combinations ,every cell with at least one N-doped component outperformed the undoped cell. The N-doped cathode with N-doped interlayer performed best, delivering 1271 mAh g-1 at 2C with the lowest charge-transfer resistance (8 Ω vs. 11 Ω undoped). Post-mortem XPS revealed Li-N interactions and polysulfide retention, strongest in the interlayers. Precursor-level nitrogen doping is therefore an effective route to Li-S cathodes and interlayers that balance nitrogen and mesoporosity.

item.title: C2 Homologation of Alkenes with Programmable Substitution
item.description: Alkene homologation represents an efficient strategy for upgrading commodity olefins and expediting the synthesis of their longer homologues. However, current alkene homologation methodologies are limited to the access to terminal alkenes. Herein, we report a radical‑based approach that enables C2 homologation of alkenes with programmable substitution patterns. This transformation features a radical hydro-alkylation of alkenes using bromomethylphosphonium hexafluorophosphate as an electrophilic carbon radical precursor. The resulting phosphonium salt, bearing a C1-extended chain, undergoes Wittig olefination with inexpensive aldehyde/ketone to deliver C2-elongated terminal/1,2-/1,1,2-substituted alkenes (>40 examples, up to 99% yield; Z/E up to >20:1, with photocatalytic access to the E-isomers). This protocol exhibits broad functional group tolerance and is applicable to the late-stage modification of bioactive compounds, pharmaceuticals, and liquid crystals. Furthermore, by iteratively combining this C2 method with our previously established C1 homologation, the olefinic chains of complex molecules can be precisely elongated by three, four, or more carbon atoms. Comprehensive mechanistic studies, including DFT calculations and experimental probes, support a radical pathway and identify hydrogen bonding between HFIP and triethylamine, which raises the competing HAT barrier from 8.5 to 13.1 kcal/mol, as the key element that suppresses reductive debromination and channels the radical toward C–C bond formation.

item.title: Techno-Economic and Geospatial Assessment of Distributed Fertilizer Production via Wastewater Ammonia Solar Electrochemical Stripping
item.description: Decentralized alternatives to centralized fertilizer production are needed to reduce supply chain risks, minimize transportation costs, and lower environmental impacts. Solar-powered Electrochemical Stripping (ECS) is an emerging technology that can produce ammonium fertilizer in a distributed manner through wastewater nitrogen recovery. We quantify the fraction of fertilizer demand in the United States that can be met by a wastewater feedstock while minimizing transportation distances, finding that 55% (5.54 Mt N per year) of demand is co-located with sufficient supply from domestic, agricultural, or industrial wastewater. A techno-economic assessment of ECS at scales sufficient to meet localized fertilizer demand estimated breakeven prices of US$8.70/kg N for ammonium sulfate, US$9.69/kg N for ammonium nitrate, and US$31.18/kg N for monoammonium phosphate, and US$12.15/kg N for diammonium phosphate. Integration of the techno-economic model with geospatial analysis found ECS-derived fertilizer prices ranged from 2.2x-5.5x local 2016-2026 retail prices, with ECS performing most competitively in the Pacific U.S. region. Sensitivity analysis showed improving current efficiency, increasing current density, lowering capital cost, and increasing equipment lifetime would have the greatest impact on approaching retail cost parity. This work elucidates pathways and barriers to widespread implementation of wastewater-derived fertilizers and advances United Nations Sustainable Development goals for responsible consumption and production, clean water, and zero hunger.

item.title: Dynamical confinement effects on chromophore photoexcitations in a light-harvesting protein
item.description: Naturally evolved light-harvesting complexes are assembled from highly evolutionarily-conserved sequences of amino acids that form functional chemical pockets for chromophores. The protein environment surrounding the chromophore influences its dynamical structure, which can have consequences for light harvesting efficiency. Here, we explore the impact of the C-phycocyanin protein scaffold on the dynamical structure and photoexcited states of the phycocyanobilin (PCB) chromophore using a combination of molecular dynamics and the ab initio Bethe Salpeter equation approach. We compute low-lying excited states of the PCB chromophore for an ensemble of snapshots from molecular dynamics trajectories, and use a normal mode analysis to understand the nature of thermal displacements of PCB in the confined protein environment. We analyze the excited state energies in terms of one electron and electron-hole contributions, identifying displacement patterns with the strongest exciton-vibrational coupling. Our results provide insight into how thermal motion of the chromophore is altered in protein environments and the resulting impact on photo-excited states, with implications for other natural light harvesting materials.
